topics.title: What is var in JavaScript?
What is let in JavaScript?
What is const in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`const` declares a block-scoped variable that cannot be reassigned after it is initialized. It must be given a value at declaration time.

---

## Explanation

`const` protects the binding, not the value. If a `const` holds an object or array, you can still change its contents; you just cannot point the name at a different object. To stop changes to the contents as well, use `Object.freeze()` or treat the data as immutable.

## Example

```ts
const user = { name: 'Aniket' };
user.name = 'Ravi';        // allowed, the object is mutated
// user = { name: 'X' };   // TypeError, the binding is constant
console.log(user.name);
```

## When to use it

Make `const` your default for every variable, and switch to `let` only when you need to reassign.

topics.title: What is the difference between var, let, and const?
topics.body:
## Know it

`var` is function-scoped, while `let` and `const` are block-scoped. `let` can be reassigned; a `const` binding cannot be reassigned. I prefer `const` by default and use `let` when the value must change.

---

## Explanation

`var` can be redeclared and is hoisted with an initial value of `undefined`. `let` and `const` are also hoisted but cannot be accessed before declaration because they are in the temporal dead zone.

## Example

```ts
const userName = 'Aniket';
let count = 0;
count += 1;
```

topics.title: What is function scope in JavaScript?
What is block scope in JavaScript?
What is the difference between function scope and block scope?
topics.body:
## Know it

Function scope means a variable is available throughout its function. Block scope means it is available only inside the block where it is declared, such as an `if` statement or loop. `var` is function-scoped; `let` and `const` are block-scoped.

---

## Explanation

Block scope helps prevent variables declared in one branch or loop from leaking into other code.

topics.title: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Hoisting describes how declarations are processed before code executes. Function declarations can be called before their definition, `var` is initialized as `undefined`, and `let`/`const` cannot be accessed before their declaration.

---

## Explanation

Do not treat `let` and `const` as usable before their declaration; that causes a temporal-dead-zone error.

## Example

```ts
sayHello();
function sayHello() { console.log('Hello'); }
```

topics.title: What is the temporal dead zone?
topics.body:
## Know it

The temporal dead zone is the period between entering a scope and the point where a `let` or `const` declaration is initialized. Accessing the variable during this period throws a `ReferenceError`.

topics.title: What is loose equality (==) in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`==` is the loose equality operator. It compares two values after converting them to a common type if the types differ.

---

## Explanation

The conversion rules are hard to remember: `'5' == 5` is true, `0 == false` is true, and `null == undefined` is true. Because of this hidden coercion, `==` can make a comparison succeed when you did not expect it to.

## Example

```ts
console.log('5' == 5);          // true, the string is converted to a number
console.log(0 == false);        // true
console.log(null == undefined); // true
console.log('' == 0);           // true
```

## When to use it

Mostly avoid it. One common accepted use is `value == null`, which checks for both `null` and `undefined` in one test.

topics.title: What is strict equality (===) in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`===` is the strict equality operator. It returns true only when both the type and the value are the same, with no type conversion.

---

## Explanation

Because it never coerces, the result is predictable: `'5' === 5` is false. For objects and arrays, `===` compares references, so two separate objects with identical contents are not strictly equal. `NaN === NaN` is false; use `Number.isNaN()` to test for it.

## Example

```ts
console.log('5' === 5);       // false, different types
console.log(5 === 5);         // true
console.log({} === {});       // false, two different objects
console.log(NaN === NaN);     // false
```

## When to use it

Use `===` and `!==` as your default for every comparison.

topics.title: What is the difference between == and ===?
topics.body:
## Know it

`==` allows type coercion before comparison, while `===` compares without converting types. I generally use `===` because it makes comparisons more predictable.

---

## Explanation

`'5' == 5` is true, but `'5' === 5` is false.

## Example

```ts
console.log('5' == 5);  // true
console.log('5' === 5); // false
```

topics.title: What is null in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`null` is a value that means "there is intentionally no value here". A developer assigns it on purpose to say a variable is empty.

---

## Explanation

`typeof null` returns `'object'`, which is a long-standing historical bug in the language. APIs often return `null` for a field that exists but has no data, for example a user without a middle name.

## Example

```ts
let selectedUser: { name: string } | null = null; // intentionally empty
console.log(selectedUser);        // null
console.log(typeof null);         // 'object' (a known quirk)
selectedUser = { name: 'Aniket' };
```

## When to use it

Use `null` to explicitly say "no value" when resetting something or when an API field is empty.

topics.title: What is undefined in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`undefined` is the value JavaScript gives automatically when something has not been given a value. It means "not assigned" rather than "empty on purpose".

---

## Explanation

You get `undefined` from a variable declared without a value, a missing object property, a function parameter that was not passed, and a function that does not return anything. `typeof undefined` is `'undefined'`.

## Example

```ts
let a;                          // declared, not assigned
const obj = { x: 1 };
function f(p?: number) { return p; }
console.log(a);                 // undefined
console.log((obj as any).y);    // undefined, property does not exist
console.log(f());               // undefined, parameter not passed
```

## When to use it

Let JavaScript produce `undefined` for missing values; avoid assigning it yourself and use `null` when you want to mean "empty on purpose".

topics.title: What is the difference between null and undefined?
topics.body:
## Know it

`undefined` commonly means a value has not been assigned or is missing. `null` is an intentional empty value. They are different values, so `null === undefined` is false.

topics.title: What are truthy and falsy values?
topics.body:
## Know it

Truthy values behave like `true` in a Boolean context; falsy values behave like `false`. Common falsy values include `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined`, and `NaN`.

---

## Explanation

Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy in JavaScript, which is a common interview trap.

topics.title: What is type coercion in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Type coercion is JavaScript's conversion of a value from one type to another, either implicitly or explicitly. For example, `==` may convert types, while `Number('12')` explicitly converts a string to a number.

topics.title: What are primitive values in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Primitive values are simple, immutable values: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `bigint`. A variable holding a primitive stores the value itself.

---

## Explanation

When you copy a primitive into another variable, you get an independent copy, so changing one does not affect the other. Primitives cannot be modified in place; operations like `'abc'.toUpperCase()` return a new value. Primitives are compared by value.

## Example

```ts
let a = 10;
let b = a;       // b gets its own copy of 10
b = 20;
console.log(a, b);           // 10 20
console.log('a' === 'a');    // true, compared by value
```

## When to use it

Primitives are the building blocks for everyday data such as names, counts, and flags. They never cause shared-state surprises.

topics.title: What are reference values in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Reference values are objects, including arrays and functions. A variable holding an object stores a reference (a pointer) to the object in memory, not a copy of it.

---

## Explanation

When you assign an object to another variable, both names point to the same object, so a change through one name is visible through the other. Two objects are equal with `===` only if they are the very same object, even when their contents look identical.

## Example

```ts
const a = { score: 1 };
const b = a;               // same object, not a copy
b.score = 99;
console.log(a.score);      // 99
console.log({ x: 1 } === { x: 1 }); // false, different objects
```

## When to use it

Objects and arrays model structured data. To avoid accidental shared changes, copy them before modifying, for example with the spread operator.

topics.title: What is the difference between primitive and reference values?
topics.body:
## Know it

Primitive values include strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, `undefined`, `bigint`, and symbols. Objects, arrays, and functions are reference values. Assigning an object variable copies the reference, not an independent object.

topics.title: What is a closure in JavaScript?
What is lexical scope in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Lexical scope means variable access is determined by where functions and blocks are written in the source code, not by where a function is called.

topics.title: How does this work in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`this` depends on how a function is called. In a method call it usually refers to the object before the dot; in an arrow function it is inherited from the surrounding lexical scope. Its behavior can differ in strict mode and when using `new`.

topics.title: What does call() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`call()` invokes a function immediately with a chosen `this` value, followed by the arguments listed one by one.

---

## Explanation

Every function has `call()`. It is useful when you want to borrow a method or run a function as if it belonged to a different object. The first argument becomes `this` inside the function.

## Example

```ts
function greet(this: any, greeting: string) {
  return greeting + ', ' + this.name;
}
const user = { name: 'Aniket' };
console.log(greet.call(user, 'Hello')); // 'Hello, Aniket'
```

## When to use it

Use it to run a function once with a specific `this`, with a fixed list of arguments.

topics.title: What does apply() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`apply()` invokes a function immediately with a chosen `this` value, like `call()`, but takes the arguments as a single array.

---

## Explanation

It is handy when the arguments are already in an array. Today the spread syntax often replaces it, for example `Math.max(...numbers)` instead of `Math.max.apply(null, numbers)`.

## Example

```ts
function add(this: any, a: number, b: number) {
  return this.base + a + b;
}
const ctx = { base: 100 };
console.log(add.apply(ctx, [1, 2])); // 103
```

## When to use it

Use it when the arguments come as an array and you also need to control `this`; otherwise prefer spread.

topics.title: What does bind() do in JavaScript?
What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`call()` invokes a function immediately with arguments listed separately. `apply()` invokes it immediately with arguments in an array-like value. `bind()` returns a new function with `this` and optionally some arguments preset.

topics.title: What is an arrow function in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

An arrow function is a shorter way to write a function using `=>`. It does not have its own `this`, `arguments`, or `prototype`; it uses `this` from the surrounding code.

---

## Explanation

Because `this` is taken from where the arrow function is written, it is a good fit for callbacks inside methods. Arrow functions cannot be used as constructors with `new`. A single-expression body returns its value without the `return` keyword.

## Example

```ts
const double = (n: number) => n * 2;
console.log(double(4)); // 8

const timer = {
  seconds: 0,
  start() { [1, 2, 3].forEach(() => { this.seconds++; }); } // `this` is the timer
};
timer.start();
console.log(timer.seconds); // 3
```

## When to use it

Use arrow functions for short callbacks and array methods. Avoid them as object methods that need their own `this`.

topics.title: What is a regular function in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A regular function is declared with the `function` keyword. It has its own `this`, which depends on how the function is called, and it can be used as a constructor with `new`.

---

## Explanation

When called as `obj.method()`, `this` is `obj`. When called on its own, `this` is `undefined` in strict mode. Regular function declarations are also hoisted, so they can be called before the line where they are defined.

## Example

```ts
function greet(this: any) { return 'Hi ' + this.name; }
const user = { name: 'Aniket', greet };
console.log(user.greet()); // 'Hi Aniket', this is user

console.log(hoisted());    // works, declarations are hoisted
function hoisted() { return 'ok'; }
```

## When to use it

Use regular functions for object methods, constructors, and any function that needs its own `this` or must be hoisted.

topics.title: What is the difference between an arrow function and a regular function?
topics.body:
## Know it

Arrow functions have lexical `this` and do not have their own `arguments` or constructor behavior. Regular functions have their own `this` based on invocation and can be used as constructors when appropriate.

topics.title: What is a higher-order function?
topics.body:
## Know it

A higher-order function accepts another function as an argument, returns a function, or both. Examples include `map()`, `filter()`, and functions that create callbacks.

topics.title: What is a pure function?
topics.body:
## Know it

A pure function returns the same output for the same inputs and does not cause observable side effects. Pure functions are easier to test and reason about.

topics.title: What is a shallow copy in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A shallow copy copies only the first level of an object or array. Nested objects and arrays inside it are still shared with the original.

---

## Explanation

The spread operator, `Object.assign()`, and `array.slice()` all make shallow copies. If you change a top-level property of the copy, the original is unaffected, but changing a nested object changes both.

## Example

```ts
const original = { name: 'A', address: { city: 'Pune' } };
const copy = { ...original };
copy.name = 'B';              // original.name is still 'A'
copy.address.city = 'Delhi';  // nested object is shared
console.log(original.address.city); // 'Delhi'
```

## When to use it

A shallow copy is enough when the data is flat, or when you will replace nested parts rather than mutate them.

topics.title: What is a deep copy in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A deep copy duplicates an object together with all nested objects and arrays, so the copy shares nothing with the original.

---

## Explanation

The modern way is `structuredClone(value)`. The old `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))` trick loses dates, `undefined`, functions, and cannot handle circular references. A deep copy costs more time and memory than a shallow copy.

## Example

```ts
const original = { name: 'A', address: { city: 'Pune' } };
const deep = structuredClone(original);
deep.address.city = 'Delhi';
console.log(original.address.city); // 'Pune', unaffected
```

## When to use it

Use it when you must change nested data without touching the source, for example editing a copy of a form model.

topics.title: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
topics.body:
## Know it

A shallow copy duplicates only the top-level structure, so nested objects remain shared references. A deep copy also duplicates nested data. The right approach depends on the data and supported value types.

topics.title: What is immutability in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Immutability means not changing an existing value directly; instead, create a new value with the desired changes. It helps make state changes easier to track, especially in UI frameworks.

topics.title: What is optional chaining?
topics.body:
## Know it

Optional chaining (`?.`) safely reads a property or calls a method only when the value before it is not `null` or `undefined`. It returns `undefined` instead of throwing for a missing intermediate value.

topics.title: What is the nullish coalescing operator (??) in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`??` returns its right-hand value only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. Other falsy values such as `0`, `''`, and `false` are kept.

---

## Explanation

This makes `??` the right choice for default values when `0`, an empty string, or `false` are valid data. It can be combined with optional chaining, for example `user?.age ?? 18`.

## Example

```ts
const count = 0;
console.log(count ?? 10);      // 0, zero is a real value
console.log(null ?? 'default'); // 'default'
console.log(undefined ?? 5);    // 5
```

## When to use it

Use it to supply a default only when a value is missing, not when it is merely falsy.

topics.title: What is the logical OR operator (||) in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`||` returns the left value if it is truthy; otherwise it returns the right value. It treats every falsy value (`0`, `''`, `false`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`) as "missing".

---

## Explanation

Using `||` for defaults is a classic bug: `0 || 10` gives `10` even though `0` may be valid. It is still the right tool in conditions, where you want "this or that is true".

## Example

```ts
console.log(0 || 10);          // 10, zero is falsy
console.log('' || 'anonymous'); // 'anonymous'
console.log('Aniket' || 'x');   // 'Aniket'
if (false || true) { console.log('at least one is true'); }
```

## When to use it

Use it in boolean conditions, or for defaults when every falsy value should be replaced.

topics.title: What is the difference between ?? and ||?
topics.body:
## Know it

`||` uses the right-hand value when the left side is falsy, including `0` and an empty string. `??` uses the fallback only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`.

topics.title: What does Object.freeze() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Object.freeze()` makes an object read-only: you cannot add, remove, or change its properties. It works on the object itself, not on a variable.

---

## Explanation

The freeze is shallow, so nested objects stay changeable unless you freeze them too. In strict mode, trying to change a frozen object throws a `TypeError`; otherwise the change is silently ignored. Use `Object.isFrozen()` to check.

## Example

```ts
const config = Object.freeze({ mode: 'dark', nested: { a: 1 } });
(config as any).mode = 'light';  // ignored (or TypeError in strict mode)
config.nested.a = 2;             // allowed, freeze is shallow
console.log(config.mode, config.nested.a); // 'dark' 2
```

## When to use it

Use it for constants and configuration objects that must never change after creation.

topics.title: What is the difference between Object.freeze() and const?
topics.body:
## Know it

`const` prevents reassignment of the variable binding but does not freeze the object. `Object.freeze()` prevents changes to an object's own properties at the top level; it is shallow unless nested values are frozen separately.

topics.title: What is destructuring in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Destructuring extracts values from arrays or properties from objects into variables. It makes code shorter when reading data from API responses, function arguments, or configuration objects.

---

## Explanation

Array destructuring uses position; object destructuring uses property names. A default value can be supplied when a property is `undefined`.

## Example

```ts
const [first, second] = ['A', 'B'];
const { name, role } = { name: 'Aniket', role: 'Developer' };
```

topics.title: What is the spread operator in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

The spread syntax (`...`) expands an iterable or an object's enumerable properties into another array or object. It is commonly used to create shallow copies or combine data.

---

## Explanation

Spread does not make a deep copy; nested objects can still be shared.

## Example

```ts
const oldUser = { name: 'A', active: false };
const newUser = { ...oldUser, active: true };
```

topics.title: What is the rest parameter in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

The rest parameter (`...args`) collects remaining function arguments into an array. Unlike spread, which expands values, rest gathers them.

---

## Explanation

The rest parameter must be the final parameter in a function declaration.

## Example

```ts
function total(...numbers) {
  return numbers.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0);
}
```

topics.title: What is the difference between spread syntax and rest syntax?
topics.body:
## Know it

They use the same `...` syntax but serve opposite purposes. Spread expands values into an array, object, or function call; rest collects remaining values into an array or object pattern.

topics.title: What is a prototype in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A prototype is an object from which another object can inherit properties and methods. JavaScript looks up a missing property along the prototype chain.

topics.title: What is prototypal inheritance?
topics.body:
## Know it

Prototypal inheritance allows one object to access properties and methods from another object through its prototype chain. JavaScript classes provide syntax over this prototype-based system.

topics.title: What is a class in JavaScript?
What is a constructor function in JavaScript?
What is the difference between a class and a constructor function?
topics.body:
## Know it

Both can create objects and share methods through prototypes. The `class` syntax provides a clearer structure and requires `new`; constructor functions use function syntax and have different invocation rules.

topics.title: What does map() do on an array in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`map()` creates a new array by running a function on every item and collecting the returned values. The new array always has the same length as the original.

---

## Explanation

`map()` does not change the original array. The callback should return a value for each item; if you forget to return, you get `undefined` entries. It is meant for transforming data, not for side effects.

## Example

```ts
const prices = [10, 20, 30];
const withTax = prices.map(p => p * 1.18);
console.log(withTax);  // [11.8, 23.6, 35.4]
console.log(prices);   // [10, 20, 30], unchanged
```

## When to use it

Use it to convert each item to something else, such as turning API objects into view models.

topics.title: What does filter() do on an array in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`filter()` returns a new array containing only the items for which the callback returns a truthy value. The result can be shorter than the original or empty.

---

## Explanation

The items themselves are not changed; they are only kept or dropped. The original array is untouched. When nothing matches, you get an empty array, not `undefined`.

## Example

```ts
const ages = [12, 18, 25, 40];
const adults = ages.filter(a => a >= 18);
console.log(adults);  // [18, 25, 40]
```

## When to use it

Use it to keep only the items that meet a condition, for example active users or items in stock.

topics.title: What does forEach() do on an array in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`forEach()` runs a function once for every item of an array. It returns `undefined`, so you cannot chain it or use its result.

---

## Explanation

It is meant for side effects such as logging or updating something outside the array. You cannot stop it early with `break`, and it does not wait for `async` callbacks. If you need a result, use `map()`, `filter()`, or `reduce()`.

## Example

```ts
const names = ['Asha', 'Ravi'];
names.forEach((n, i) => console.log(i + ': ' + n));
const result = names.forEach(n => n);
console.log(result);  // undefined
```

## When to use it

Use it when you only need to do something for each item and do not need a new array.

topics.title: What is the difference between map(), filter(), and forEach()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`map()` returns a new array with each element transformed. `filter()` returns a new array containing elements that pass a condition. `forEach()` runs a callback for each element and does not build a transformed array.

topics.title: What does find() do on an array in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`find()` returns the first item for which the callback returns true, or `undefined` if there is no match. It stops as soon as it finds one.

---

## Explanation

Because it stops early, it is cheaper than `filter()` when you only need one item. Always handle the `undefined` case. If you need the position instead of the item, use `findIndex()`.

## Example

```ts
const users = [{ id: 1, name: 'A' }, { id: 2, name: 'B' }];
const user = users.find(u => u.id === 2);
console.log(user);  // { id: 2, name: 'B' }
console.log(users.find(u => u.id === 9)); // undefined
```

## When to use it

Use it to look up a single item, such as a record by id.

topics.title: What is the difference between find() and filter()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`find()` returns the first matching element, or `undefined` if there is no match. `filter()` returns an array containing every matching element, which may be empty.

topics.title: What does reduce() do on an array in JavaScript?
What is the difference between reduce() and map()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`map()` transforms every item and returns an array of the same length. `reduce()` accumulates items into a single result, such as a number, object, or grouped collection.

topics.title: Which array method would you use to check whether any item matches a condition?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use `some()` when you need a Boolean indicating whether at least one item passes a condition. Use `every()` when all items must pass.

topics.title: What does slice() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`slice(start, end)` returns a shallow copy of part of an array (or string) without changing the original. The `end` index is not included.

---

## Explanation

Negative indexes count from the end, and `slice()` with no arguments copies the whole array. Since the original is untouched, it is safe to use on state that must not be mutated.

## Example

```ts
const letters = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'];
console.log(letters.slice(1, 3));  // ['b', 'c']
console.log(letters.slice(-2));    // ['c', 'd']
console.log(letters);              // unchanged
```

## When to use it

Use it to take a portion of an array, make a quick copy, or take the last few items without mutation.

topics.title: What does splice() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` changes the original array by removing, replacing, or inserting items at a position. It returns an array of the removed items.

---

## Explanation

Because it mutates the array in place, it can cause bugs in shared data or framework state that expects a new array. To get a modified copy without changing the original, use `slice()`, spread, or `toSpliced()`.

## Example

```ts
const items = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'];
const removed = items.splice(1, 2, 'X');
console.log(removed);  // ['b', 'c']
console.log(items);    // ['a', 'X', 'd'], the original changed
```

## When to use it

Use it when you really want to edit an array in place, such as inserting or deleting at a known index in local data.

topics.title: What is the difference between slice() and splice()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`slice()` returns a selected portion without modifying the original array. `splice()` adds, removes, or replaces items in the original array.

topics.title: What is for...of in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`for...of` loops over the values of an iterable such as an array, string, `Map`, or `Set`. You get each item directly.

---

## Explanation

It works with anything that implements the iterable protocol and supports `break`, `continue`, and `await` inside the loop. It does not work on plain objects, because they are not iterable.

## Example

```ts
for (const value of ['a', 'b', 'c']) {
  console.log(value);   // a, b, c
}
for (const ch of 'hi') console.log(ch); // h, i
```

## When to use it

Use it to loop over the values of arrays, strings, maps, and sets.

topics.title: What is for...in in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`for...in` loops over the enumerable property names (keys) of an object, as strings. It also includes inherited enumerable properties.

---

## Explanation

On arrays it gives the indexes as strings and may include extra properties, so it is a poor choice for arrays. When looping over an object, use `Object.keys()`, `Object.values()`, or `Object.entries()` for clearer control.

## Example

```ts
const user = { name: 'Aniket', age: 30 };
for (const key in user) {
  console.log(key);   // 'name', 'age'
}
console.log(Object.entries(user)); // [['name','Aniket'],['age',30]]
```

## When to use it

Use it only to inspect the keys of a plain object, and prefer `Object.entries()` in most cases.

topics.title: What is the difference between for...of and for...in?
topics.body:
## Know it

`for...of` iterates over values from an iterable such as an array. `for...in` iterates over enumerable property keys, so it is generally more appropriate for object keys than array values.

topics.title: What is a Set and when would you use it?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `Set` stores unique values. It is useful for removing duplicate primitive values or checking membership without manually searching an array.

topics.title: What is a plain object used as a dictionary in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A plain object stores key-value pairs where keys are strings or symbols. It is the default structure for records and for quick lookups.

---

## Explanation

Any other key type is converted to a string, so `1` and `'1'` are the same key. Plain objects inherit properties such as `toString`, which can clash with data keys. Their size is not available directly, and insertion order is only reliable for non-numeric keys.

## Example

```ts
const stock: Record<string, number> = { apple: 5, pear: 2 };
stock.banana = 7;
console.log(Object.keys(stock).length); // 3
console.log('apple' in stock);          // true
```

## When to use it

Use it for fixed, known shapes like a user record, or for simple string-keyed lookups.

topics.title: What is a Map in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `Map` is a built-in collection of key-value pairs where keys can be any type, including objects and functions. It remembers the order in which entries were added.

---

## Explanation

A `Map` has a `size` property, and `get`, `set`, `has`, and `delete` methods. It is directly iterable with `for...of`. It has no inherited keys, so it is safer for dictionaries with unpredictable keys, and it is usually faster when you add and remove entries often.

## Example

```ts
const roles = new Map<number, string>();
roles.set(1, 'admin');
roles.set(2, 'user');
console.log(roles.get(1));  // 'admin'
console.log(roles.size);    // 2
for (const [id, role] of roles) console.log(id, role);
```

## When to use it

Use it when keys are not simple strings, when order matters, or when you add and delete entries frequently.

topics.title: What is a Map and how is it different from a plain object?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `Map` stores key-value pairs and allows keys of any value type, preserves insertion order, and exposes a `size` property. Plain objects are often best for records with known string or symbol keys.

topics.title: What does JSON.stringify() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`JSON.stringify(value)` converts a JavaScript value into a JSON text string, so it can be sent over a network, stored, or logged.

---

## Explanation

Functions, `undefined`, and symbols are skipped, `Date` objects become strings, and circular references throw an error. An optional second argument filters properties and a third argument adds indentation for readability.

## Example

```ts
const user = { name: 'Aniket', age: 30, skills: ['js', 'ts'] };
const text = JSON.stringify(user);
console.log(text);                       // '{"name":"Aniket","age":30,"skills":["js","ts"]}'
console.log(JSON.stringify(user, null, 2)); // pretty printed
```

## When to use it

Use it when saving data to localStorage or sending a request body.

topics.title: What does JSON.parse() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`JSON.parse(text)` converts a JSON string back into a JavaScript value such as an object or array. It throws a `SyntaxError` if the text is not valid JSON.

---

## Explanation

Always wrap it in `try/catch` when the text comes from outside your code. The result is untyped, so in TypeScript validate its shape before trusting it. Dates stay as strings and need to be converted by hand or with a reviver function.

## Example

```ts
const text = '{"name":"Aniket","age":30}';
const user = JSON.parse(text);
console.log(user.name);  // 'Aniket'
try { JSON.parse('{ bad json'); } catch (e) { console.log('invalid JSON'); }
```

## When to use it

Use it to read stored data or an API response that arrives as text.

topics.title: What is the difference between JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`JSON.stringify()` converts a JavaScript value into JSON text. `JSON.parse()` converts valid JSON text into a JavaScript value. Not every JavaScript value is preserved by JSON serialization.

topics.title: What is event bubbling?
topics.body:
## Know it

Event bubbling means an event triggered on a nested element can propagate upward through its ancestors. Event delegation uses this behavior to handle events from many child elements with one parent listener.

topics.title: What is event delegation?
topics.body:
## Know it

Event delegation attaches one listener to a parent and uses the event target to identify which child triggered the event. It can reduce listeners and work well for dynamic lists.

topics.title: What does preventDefault() do in JavaScript?
What does stopPropagation() do in JavaScript?
What is the difference between preventDefault() and stopPropagation()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`preventDefault()` prevents the browser's default action when the event is cancelable. `stopPropagation()` stops the event from continuing through the propagation path. They solve different problems.

topics.title: What is synchronous code in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Synchronous code runs line by line, and each statement must finish before the next one starts. While it runs, JavaScript can do nothing else.

---

## Explanation

JavaScript runs on a single thread, so a long synchronous task, like a huge loop, blocks the page: clicks and rendering freeze until it finishes. Short, quick operations are fine to run synchronously.

## Example

```ts
console.log('first');
for (let i = 0; i < 1e6; i++) {}   // blocks until done
console.log('second');            // runs only after the loop
```

## When to use it

Use synchronous code for quick calculations and simple logic, where waiting does not matter.

topics.title: What is asynchronous code in JavaScript?
What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous code?
topics.body:
## Know it

Synchronous code executes step by step and blocks the current flow until each operation finishes. Asynchronous code lets work such as network requests finish later so other work can continue.

topics.title: What is the event loop in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

The event loop coordinates the call stack with queued work. After the current synchronous code completes, microtasks such as Promise callbacks are processed before the next task such as a timer callback.

topics.title: What is a callback in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A callback is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later, often when an asynchronous task finishes.

---

## Explanation

Callbacks are simple but can get hard to manage: nested callbacks form a "callback hell" pyramid, error handling must be repeated at every level, and it is easy to call the callback twice or never.

## Example

```ts
function loadUser(id: number, done: (user: { id: number }) => void) {
  setTimeout(() => done({ id }), 100);
}
loadUser(1, user => console.log('loaded', user.id));
```

## When to use it

Use callbacks for simple, one-step cases such as event handlers and array methods like `map()`.

topics.title: What is a Promise in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A Promise is an object that represents a value that will be available later. It is either pending, fulfilled with a value, or rejected with an error.

---

## Explanation

You attach handlers with `.then()`, `.catch()`, and `.finally()`, and Promises can be chained to run steps in order. Errors travel down the chain to one `.catch()`. A Promise settles once and then never changes, and `async/await` is syntax built on top of it.

## Example

```ts
const wait = (ms: number) => new Promise<string>(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve('done'), ms));
wait(50)
  .then(value => { console.log(value); })
  .catch(error => console.log('failed', error))
  .finally(() => console.log('cleanup'));
```

## When to use it

Use Promises (usually with `async/await`) for one-time asynchronous results such as an HTTP request.

topics.title: What is the difference between a Promise and a callback?
topics.body:
## Know it

A callback is a function passed to another function to be called later or during an operation. A Promise represents the eventual success or failure of an asynchronous operation and supports chaining with `then`, `catch`, and `finally`.

topics.title: What are the states of a Promise?
topics.body:
## Know it

A Promise can be pending, fulfilled, or rejected. Once it is fulfilled or rejected, it is settled and cannot change to another state.

topics.title: What does Promise.all() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Promise.all()` takes several Promises and returns one Promise that resolves with an array of all results, in order, when every Promise succeeds. It rejects as soon as any one of them rejects.

---

## Explanation

All the Promises run at the same time, so the total time is roughly the slowest one. When one fails, you get that single error and lose the other results (although those tasks still continue running).

## Example

```ts
const wait = (ms: number, v: string) => new Promise<string>(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
const results = await Promise.all([wait(30, 'a'), wait(10, 'b')]);
console.log(results);  // ['a', 'b'], same order as the input
```

## When to use it

Use it when you need every result and one failure should fail the whole operation, for example loading the data a page cannot render without.

topics.title: What does Promise.allSettled() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Promise.allSettled()` waits for every Promise to finish, whether fulfilled or rejected, and gives an array describing each outcome. It never rejects.

---

## Explanation

Each entry looks like `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }`. This lets you handle partial success, for example showing the data that loaded and an error for the part that failed.

## Example

```ts
const ok = Promise.resolve('data');
const bad = Promise.reject(new Error('failed'));
const outcomes = await Promise.allSettled([ok, bad]);
console.log(outcomes.map(o => o.status));  // ['fulfilled', 'rejected']
```

## When to use it

Use it when the tasks are independent and you want all results even if some fail, such as a dashboard made of several widgets.

topics.title: What is the difference between Promise.all() and Promise.allSettled()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Promise.all()` fulfills when all promises fulfill and rejects as soon as one rejects. `Promise.allSettled()` waits for all promises and reports each result as fulfilled or rejected.

topics.title: What does Promise.race() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Promise.race()` settles as soon as the first of the given Promises settles, whether that is a success or a failure. The result is the outcome of that first one.

---

## Explanation

If the fastest Promise rejects, `race()` rejects too. The other Promises are not cancelled; their results are simply ignored. A common use is adding a timeout.

## Example

```ts
const wait = (ms: number, v: string) => new Promise<string>(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
const winner = await Promise.race([wait(100, 'slow'), wait(20, 'fast')]);
console.log(winner);  // 'fast'
```

## When to use it

Use it for timeouts, or when you only care about whichever source answers first, success or failure.

topics.title: What does Promise.any() do in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Promise.any()` resolves with the value of the first Promise that fulfills. It ignores rejections until all Promises have rejected, and then it rejects with an `AggregateError`.

---

## Explanation

This makes it good for redundancy: try several sources and use the first success. An error only appears if every single attempt fails.

## Example

```ts
const fail = Promise.reject(new Error('down'));
const good = new Promise<string>(r => setTimeout(() => r('mirror B'), 20));
console.log(await Promise.any([fail, good]));  // 'mirror B'
```

## When to use it

Use it to request the same data from several servers or mirrors and take the first one that works.

topics.title: What is the difference between Promise.race() and Promise.any()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Promise.race()` settles with the first promise that settles, whether fulfilled or rejected. `Promise.any()` fulfills with the first fulfilled promise and rejects only if all input promises reject.

topics.title: What is async/await?
topics.body:
## Know it

`async` makes a function return a Promise, and `await` pauses that async function until a Promise settles. It lets asynchronous code read more like sequential code; it does not make the operation itself synchronous.

topics.title: How should errors be handled with async/await?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use `try/catch` around awaited operations when you need to handle rejection locally. If the error cannot be handled there, rethrow it or let the caller handle the rejected Promise.

topics.title: What are microtasks in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Microtasks are small jobs that run right after the current code finishes, before the browser renders or handles the next macrotask. Promise callbacks (`.then`, `await` continuations) and `queueMicrotask()` create them.

---

## Explanation

The event loop empties the whole microtask queue after each task. Because of this, microtasks always run before timers, even `setTimeout(fn, 0)`. A microtask that keeps adding more microtasks can starve the page.

## Example

```ts
console.log('1 sync');
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('2 microtask'));
console.log('3 sync');
// 1 sync, 3 sync, 2 microtask
```

## When to use it

Use them (through Promises) for work that must happen right after the current code but before anything else.

topics.title: What are macrotasks in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Macrotasks (also called tasks) are larger units of work scheduled by the browser or Node, such as `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, user events, and I/O callbacks. The event loop runs one macrotask at a time.

---

## Explanation

After each macrotask, all pending microtasks run, then the browser may render, and then the next macrotask starts. Even `setTimeout(fn, 0)` waits for at least the next turn of the loop.

## Example

```ts
setTimeout(() => console.log('macrotask: timer'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('microtask: promise'));
console.log('sync');
// sync, microtask: promise, macrotask: timer
```

## When to use it

Use timers when you want to let the browser breathe, for example splitting heavy work into chunks so the page stays responsive.

topics.title: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks?
topics.body:
## Know it

Promise reactions and `queueMicrotask()` run in the microtask queue. Timers such as `setTimeout()` schedule tasks. After synchronous code, the runtime generally drains microtasks before moving to the next task.

topics.title: Why can setTimeout(fn, 0) run after a Promise callback?
topics.body:
## Know it

A zero-delay timer schedules a task; it does not run immediately. Promise callbacks are microtasks, which are generally processed before the next timer task.

topics.title: What is debouncing?
topics.body:
## Know it

Debouncing delays an action until a period of inactivity has passed. It is useful for search inputs so the app does not send a request after every keystroke.

topics.title: What is throttling?
topics.body:
## Know it

Throttling limits how often a function can run during a time window. It is useful for frequent events such as scrolling or resizing.

topics.title: What is the difference between debouncing and throttling?
topics.body:
## Know it

Debouncing waits until activity pauses before running. Throttling allows execution at a controlled maximum frequency while activity continues.

topics.title: What is the difference between Promise and Observable?
topics.body:
## Know it

A Promise typically produces one eventual success or failure result. An Observable can emit multiple values over time and can be transformed with RxJS operators; many Observables start on subscription.

topics.title: How can you run independent asynchronous requests in parallel?
topics.body:
## Know it

Start the independent requests together and await a grouping method such as `Promise.all()`. This avoids waiting for each request sequentially, while still handling failures appropriately.

topics.title: What is a race condition in asynchronous JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A race condition occurs when the result depends on the order or timing of asynchronous operations. For example, an older search request may finish after a newer request and overwrite its result.

topics.title: How do you remove duplicate values from an array?
topics.body:
## Know it

For an array of primitive values, `Array.from(new Set(values))` or `[...new Set(values)]` returns unique values. Objects require a rule for what makes two objects duplicates.

topics.title: How do you group an array of objects by a property?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use `reduce()` to build an object or `Map` keyed by the chosen property. Keep the grouping logic clear and handle missing property values if they are possible.

topics.title: How do you safely copy an object before updating one property?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use object spread to create a shallow copy and override the property. If nested data is updated, copy the relevant nested objects too so the original state is not accidentally mutated.

topics.title: What is optional chaining useful for when reading API data?
topics.body:
## Know it

Optional chaining lets code safely read nested response properties that may be missing, such as `response.customer?.address?.city`. It avoids an error for nullish intermediate values but does not validate the response shape.

topics.title: How do you sort an array of numbers correctly?
topics.body:
## Know it

Pass a numeric comparator to `sort()`, such as `(a, b) => a - b`, because the default sort compares string representations. Remember that `sort()` mutates the original array.

topics.title: What are mutating array methods in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Mutating array methods change the original array in place. Common ones are `push`, `pop`, `shift`, `unshift`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse`, and `fill`.

---

## Explanation

Changing shared data can cause hidden bugs, and in frameworks like Angular with `OnPush` or signals, an in-place change may not be detected. Note that `sort()` and `reverse()` also mutate, which surprises many developers.

## Example

```ts
const nums = [3, 1, 2];
nums.push(4);       // mutates
nums.sort();        // mutates, now [1, 2, 3, 4]
console.log(nums);
```

## When to use it

Use them on local arrays you own and no one else reads, or when performance matters and the mutation is contained.

topics.title: What are non-mutating array methods in JavaScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Non-mutating array methods leave the original array unchanged and return a new array or value. Common ones are `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`, spread, `reduce`, and the newer `toSorted`, `toReversed`, and `toSpliced`.

---

## Explanation

Because the source stays intact, the code is easier to reason about and works well with change detection that compares references. To sort without mutating, copy first with `[...array].sort()` or use `toSorted()`.

## Example

```ts
const nums = [3, 1, 2];
const sorted = [...nums].sort((a, b) => a - b);
console.log(sorted);  // [1, 2, 3]
console.log(nums);    // [3, 1, 2], unchanged
```

## When to use it

Use them by default for state and shared data, so a change always produces a new array.

topics.title: What is the difference between mutable and immutable array methods?
topics.body:
## Know it

Mutating methods such as `push()`, `splice()`, and `sort()` change the original array. Methods such as `map()`, `filter()`, and `slice()` return a new array. Some newer methods like `toSorted()` return a sorted copy.

topics.title: What is TypeScript and why use it in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

TypeScript adds static type checking and language features on top of JavaScript. In Angular, it helps catch many mistakes during development, documents component and API data shapes, and improves editor support.

topics.title: What is the any type in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`any` turns off type checking for a value. TypeScript will let you do anything with it: call it, read any property, or pass it anywhere.

---

## Explanation

That freedom removes the safety TypeScript is meant to give, so mistakes only show up at runtime. `any` also spreads: a value computed from an `any` is usually `any` too. It exists mainly for migrating old JavaScript code.

## Example

```ts
let data: any = 'hello';
data = 42;                 // allowed, any accepts everything
console.log(data.toFixed(1)); // '42.0'
data = 'text';
// data.toFixed(1);        // compiles fine, but crashes at runtime
console.log(typeof data);
```

## When to use it

Avoid it. Use it only as a short-lived escape hatch, for example while migrating a file, and prefer `unknown` or a real type.

topics.title: What is the unknown type in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`unknown` is the safe version of `any`. A value of type `unknown` can hold anything, but you must check its type before you can use it.

---

## Explanation

TypeScript refuses to let you call methods or read properties on an `unknown` until you narrow it, for example with `typeof`, `instanceof`, or a type guard. This forces you to handle data you do not trust, such as parsed JSON or a caught error.

## Example

```ts
function describe(value: unknown): string {
  if (typeof value === 'string') return 'text of length ' + value.length;
  if (typeof value === 'number') return 'number ' + value.toFixed(1);
  return 'something else';
}
console.log(describe('hello'));  // text of length 5
console.log(describe(42));       // number 42.0
console.log(describe(true));     // something else
```

## When to use it

Use it for values whose type you do not know yet, such as API data, `JSON.parse()` results, and `catch` errors.

topics.title: What is the difference between any and unknown?
topics.body:
## Know it

`any` disables most type checking for a value. `unknown` can hold any value, but you must narrow or validate its type before using it. I prefer `unknown` when the input type is not yet known.

topics.title: What is the never type in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`never` represents values that should never occur, such as a function that always throws or an exhaustive branch that cannot be reached. It is also useful for checking that all union cases have been handled.

topics.title: What is an interface in TypeScript?
What is a type alias in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `type` alias gives a name to any type: an object shape, a union, a tuple, a function type, or a computed type.

---

## Explanation

Type aliases are more flexible than interfaces because they can describe unions, intersections, tuples, and mapped or conditional types. They cannot be merged by declaring them twice. Objects can also be combined with `&` (intersection).

## Example

```ts
type Status = 'pending' | 'success' | 'failed';       // union
type Point = [number, number];                         // tuple
type Callback = (value: string) => void;               // function type
type Named = { name: string } & { age: number };       // intersection

const s: Status = 'success';
const p: Point = [10, 20];
console.log(s, p);
```

## When to use it

Use it for unions, tuples, function types, and any type that is not a plain object shape.

topics.title: What is the difference between interface and type?
topics.body:
## Know it

Both can describe object shapes. Interfaces can be extended and declaration-merged; type aliases can represent unions, intersections, primitives, tuples, and other type expressions. I choose based on the shape and use case.

topics.title: What is a union type?
topics.body:
## Know it

A union type allows a value to be one of several types, such as `string | number`. Before using a member-specific operation, the code should narrow the value to the appropriate type.

topics.title: What is type narrowing?
topics.body:
## Know it

Type narrowing is using checks such as `typeof`, `in`, equality checks, or custom type guards to make TypeScript understand that a value has a more specific type within a code path.

topics.title: What is a type guard?
topics.body:
## Know it

A type guard is a check that narrows a value's type, such as `typeof value === 'string'`, `instanceof`, or a custom function returning `value is SomeType`.

topics.title: What is an optional property in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

An optional property is marked with `?` and may be missing from the object entirely. Its type is the declared type plus `undefined`.

---

## Explanation

You can leave the property out when creating the object, and when reading it you must handle `undefined`. It is a good fit for fields that may not be provided, such as an optional filter.

## Example

```ts
interface Settings {
  theme: string;
  pageSize?: number;   // may be missing
}
const a: Settings = { theme: 'dark' };                 // fine, pageSize omitted
const b: Settings = { theme: 'light', pageSize: 20 };
console.log(a.pageSize ?? 10);  // 10, default when missing
console.log(b.pageSize ?? 10);  // 20
```

## When to use it

Use it for properties that callers are allowed to leave out.

topics.title: What is a nullable property in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A nullable property has a type that includes `null`, such as `string | null`. The property must be present, but its value may be `null`.

---

## Explanation

This models data where the field always exists but may be empty, which is common in APIs: for example `middleName: null`. You must check for `null` before using the value, and with `strictNullChecks` TypeScript enforces that.

## Example

```ts
interface Person {
  name: string;
  middleName: string | null;   // always present, may be null
}
const p: Person = { name: 'Aniket', middleName: null };
console.log(p.middleName?.toUpperCase() ?? 'no middle name'); // 'no middle name'
```

## When to use it

Use it when the field is always sent but can be empty, to represent "no value" explicitly.

topics.title: What is the difference between optional properties and nullable properties?
topics.body:
## Know it

An optional property may be absent or `undefined`, depending on compiler settings. A nullable property explicitly allows values such as `null`, for example `name: string | null`. These represent different API contracts.

topics.title: What is readonly in TypeScript?
What is the difference between readonly and const?
topics.body:
## Know it

`const` prevents reassignment of a variable binding. `readonly` prevents assignment to a property through that typed reference after initialization. Both are compile-time constraints and do not deeply freeze runtime objects.

topics.title: What are generics in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Generics let functions, classes, and interfaces work with different types while preserving type information. They help create reusable APIs without falling back to `any`.

topics.title: What is a generic constraint?
topics.body:
## Know it

A generic constraint limits which types can be supplied to a generic parameter, often using `extends`. It allows the implementation to safely access the members guaranteed by that constraint.

topics.title: What are TypeScript utility types?
topics.body:
## Know it

Utility types transform existing types. Common examples include `Partial<T>`, `Required<T>`, `Pick<T, K>`, `Omit<T, K>`, `Readonly<T>`, and `Record<K, V>`.

topics.title: What is the Pick utility type in TypeScript?
What is the Omit utility type in TypeScript?
What is the difference between Pick and Omit?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Pick<T, K>` creates a type with selected properties. `Omit<T, K>` creates a type with the specified properties excluded.

topics.title: What is Record<K, V> used for?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Record<K, V>` describes an object whose keys are of type `K` and whose values are of type `V`. It is useful for typed lookup dictionaries and configuration maps.

topics.title: What is keyof in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`keyof T` produces a union of the keys of type `T`. It is often used in generic functions to restrict a key parameter to valid property names.

topics.title: What is typeof in TypeScript type positions?
topics.body:
## Know it

In a type position, `typeof` obtains the type of an existing value. It is useful when a type should stay aligned with a constant or object defined in code.

topics.title: What is as const in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`as const` asks TypeScript to infer literal types and readonly properties for an expression instead of widening values to general types. It affects type checking, not runtime freezing.

topics.title: What is a discriminated union?
topics.body:
## Know it

A discriminated union is a union of object types that share a literal property, such as `kind`. Checking that property narrows the object to the matching variant and supports exhaustive handling.

topics.title: What is type assertion, and when should you avoid it?
topics.body:
## Know it

A type assertion tells TypeScript to treat a value as a specified type, but it does not validate the value at runtime. Avoid using assertions to hide uncertain API data; prefer validation and narrowing.

topics.title: What is an enum in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

An `enum` defines a named set of constants. A numeric enum maps names to numbers; a string enum maps names to strings.

---

## Explanation

Unlike most TypeScript features, an enum produces real JavaScript code (an object) at runtime. Numeric enums also allow reverse lookup from number to name. Because of the generated code, some teams prefer string-literal unions for simple cases.

## Example

```ts
enum Direction {
  Up,
  Down,
}
enum Role {
  Admin = 'ADMIN',
  User = 'USER',
}
console.log(Direction.Down);   // 1
console.log(Direction[0]);     // 'Up', reverse lookup
console.log(Role.Admin);       // 'ADMIN'
```

## When to use it

Use it when you want a runtime object of named constants that you can also iterate or look up.

topics.title: What is a union of string literals in TypeScript?
What is the difference between an enum and a union of string literals?
topics.body:
## Know it

An enum creates a named TypeScript enum construct, with runtime output depending on the enum kind. A string-literal union provides a set of allowed literal values mainly at type level. Choose based on runtime needs and project conventions.

topics.title: What is structural typing in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

TypeScript mostly checks compatibility by the structure of values—their members—rather than by explicit class or interface names. If the required members match, values may be compatible.

topics.title: What is function overload in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Function overloads provide multiple public call signatures for different argument combinations, followed by one implementation. They are useful when the return type depends on the input pattern.

topics.title: What is a type error in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

A type error is a mistake that the TypeScript compiler reports before the program runs, such as passing a string where a number is required.

---

## Explanation

Type errors are found during compilation or in the editor, so they cost almost nothing to fix. They tell you that the code may misuse a value; if you ignore them (for example with `any` or `as`), the problem can still happen at runtime.

## Example

```ts
function double(n: number): number {
  return n * 2;
}
// double('5');        // compile-time type error: string is not a number
console.log(double(5));  // 10
```

## When to use it

Treat type errors as free, early bug reports and fix them instead of silencing them.

topics.title: What is a runtime error in JavaScript and TypeScript?
What is the difference between a type error and a runtime error?
topics.body:
## Know it

A type error is reported by TypeScript during development or compilation. A runtime error happens while the JavaScript executes, for example when accessing a property on `undefined`. TypeScript types do not automatically validate external data at runtime.

topics.title: What does extends do in TypeScript?
What does implements do in TypeScript?
What is the difference between extends and implements in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`extends` inherits from a class or builds on a type/interface. `implements` checks that a class satisfies an interface or object type contract; it does not copy implementation code from that interface.

topics.title: What are access modifiers in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`public` is accessible broadly, `private` restricts access to the class, and `protected` allows access in the class and subclasses. TypeScript's `private` is primarily a type-checking restriction; ECMAScript `#private` fields provide runtime privacy.

topics.title: What is dependency inversion at the TypeScript design level?
topics.body:
## Know it

Dependency inversion means higher-level code depends on an abstraction rather than a specific implementation. In TypeScript, interfaces or abstract classes can describe the contract, while concrete implementations provide behavior.

topics.title: What are compile-time types in TypeScript?
What are runtime values in JavaScript and TypeScript?
What is the difference between compile-time types and runtime values?
topics.body:
## Know it

TypeScript types are erased during compilation, while JavaScript values exist at runtime. An interface cannot be checked with `instanceof`; runtime validation needs actual values or validation logic.

topics.title: How do you type an API response in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

Define an interface or type for the expected response and use it as the `HttpClient` generic where appropriate. Remember that the generic is a compile-time assumption, not runtime validation of the server response.

topics.title: What is a component in Angular?
What is a service in Angular?
What is the difference between a component and a service in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A component manages a view and its interaction. A service contains reusable business logic or shared functionality and is commonly injected into components or other services.

topics.title: What is dependency injection in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Dependency injection lets Angular provide a class with the dependencies it needs rather than having the class create them directly. It improves reuse, testability, and separation of concerns.

topics.title: What does providedIn: 'root' mean in Angular?
What are component-level providers in Angular?
What is the difference between providedIn: 'root' and component-level providers?
topics.body:
## Know it

`providedIn: 'root'` normally makes one application-level service instance available through the root injector. A component-level provider creates a service instance in that component's injector scope, which can be useful for isolated state.

topics.title: What is the constructor in an Angular component?
What is ngOnInit in Angular?
What is the difference between constructor and ngOnInit?
topics.body:
## Know it

The constructor is for class initialization and receiving injected dependencies. `ngOnInit` runs after Angular initializes the component's input properties and is commonly used for setup that depends on those inputs.

topics.title: What is ngOnChanges in Angular?
What is the difference between ngOnInit and ngOnChanges?
topics.body:
## Know it

`ngOnInit` runs once after initial input setup. `ngOnChanges` runs when Angular detects changes to data-bound inputs, including the initial input setting, so it is useful when behavior must respond to input changes.

topics.title: What is ngAfterViewInit in Angular?
What is ngAfterViewChecked in Angular?
What is the difference between ngAfterViewInit and ngAfterViewChecked?
topics.body:
## Know it

`ngAfterViewInit` runs once after the component view and its child views are initialized. `ngAfterViewChecked` runs after Angular checks the view, so it can run frequently and should be used cautiously.

topics.title: What is @Input in Angular?
What is @Output in Angular?
What is the difference between @Input and @Output?
topics.body:
## Know it

`@Input` passes data from a parent component to a child. `@Output` emits an event from a child so the parent can respond.

topics.title: What is ViewChild in Angular?
What is ViewChildren in Angular?
What is the difference between ViewChild and ViewChildren?
topics.body:
## Know it

`ViewChild` queries for one matching element or child and returns one reference. `ViewChildren` returns a `QueryList` of matching elements or children and is appropriate when there may be multiple matches.

topics.title: What is ng-content in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `` is a placeholder inside a component's template where content supplied by the parent is shown. This is called content projection. --- ## Explanation It makes components flexible, like reusable cards and dialogs that let the parent decide what goes inside. With a `select` attribute you can define several slots, for example one for the header and one for the body. ## Example ```text // card.component.html

Profile

This text is projected into the body.

 ``` ## When to use it Use it for reusable wrapper components where the parent supplies the inner content.

topics.title: What is ng-template in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `` defines a piece of HTML that Angular does not render by itself. It is rendered only when something uses it, such as `*ngIf` with `else`, `ngTemplateOutlet`, or a structural directive. --- ## Explanation Think of it as a stored blueprint. The same template can be rendered several times or conditionally, and it can receive context data. Structural directives like `*ngIf` are shorthand that create an `ng-template` behind the scenes. ## Example ```text
Hello {{ user.name }}

Loading...

 ``` ## When to use it Use it for content that should appear only on demand, for `else` branches, and for templates you pass around.

topics.title: What is ng-container in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `` is a grouping element that Angular does not add to the page. It lets you attach structural directives to a group of elements without creating an extra wrapper tag. --- ## Explanation It avoids unnecessary `div` elements that can break layout or CSS. It is especially helpful because an element can only have one structural directive, so you can place `*ngIf` on the container and `*ngFor` on the child. ## Example ```text
  • {{ item }}
    •  ``` ## When to use it Use it when you need a directive on a group of elements but do not want extra markup.

topics.title: What is the difference between ng-content, ng-template, and ng-container?
topics.body:
## Know it

`ng-content` projects content supplied by a parent. `ng-template` defines a template that is rendered later or conditionally. `ng-container` groups template nodes without adding a real DOM element.

topics.title: What is a standalone component in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A standalone component declares its template dependencies through its own `imports` and does not need to be declared in an NgModule. Standalone APIs simplify composition and application bootstrapping.

topics.title: What is change detection in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Change detection is Angular's process for checking component bindings and updating the view when application state changes. Component strategy and the way state is updated can affect when checks occur.

topics.title: What is Default change detection in Angular?
What is OnPush change detection in Angular?
What is the difference between Default and OnPush change detection?
topics.body:
## Know it

Default checks a component as part of normal change-detection runs. OnPush allows Angular to skip checks in more situations and checks the component when relevant triggers occur, such as changed input references, events in its subtree, or explicit notification.

topics.title: What are Angular signals?
topics.body:
## Know it

Signals are reactive values that notify Angular when their value changes. `signal()` stores writable state, `computed()` derives state, and `effect()` runs side effects in response to signal dependencies.

topics.title: What is signal() in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `signal()` creates a writable reactive value. You read it by calling it like a function, and change it with `set()` or `update()`. Angular knows exactly where it is used, so only those parts update. --- ## Explanation A signal always has a value, and reading `count()` inside a template or `computed` creates a dependency. Updating the signal notifies those dependents automatically. This gives fine-grained updates without relying on Zone.js checks. ## Example ```text const count = signal(0); console.log(count()); // 0 (read by calling it) count.set(5); // replace the value count.update(c => c + 1); // change based on the old value console.log(count()); // 6 // template:

{{ count() }}

updates automatically ``` ## When to use it Use it for local, writable state in a component or service.

topics.title: What is computed() in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`computed()` creates a read-only signal whose value is derived from other signals. It recalculates automatically, but only when one of its dependencies changes.

---

## Explanation

The result is cached (memoized): reading it again without a change returns the stored value with no recalculation. You cannot set a `computed` directly. It replaces repeated calls to expensive methods in templates.

## Example

```text
const price = signal(100);
const quantity = signal(2);
const total = computed(() => price() * quantity());

console.log(total());   // 200
quantity.set(3);
console.log(total());   // 300, recalculated automatically
```

## When to use it

Use it for values that are calculated from other state, such as totals, filtered lists, and flags.

topics.title: What is effect() in Angular?
What is the difference between signal(), computed(), and effect()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`signal()` stores writable reactive state. `computed()` derives a read-only value from other signals. `effect()` runs side-effect code when the signals it reads change and should not be used as a general replacement for derived state.

topics.title: What is an InjectionToken in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

An `InjectionToken` lets Angular inject a value that does not have a class type, such as configuration, a function, or an interface-backed value. It provides a runtime token for a dependency.

topics.title: What is useClass in Angular providers?
topics.body:
## Know it

`useClass` tells Angular which class to create when something asks for a token. It lets you provide a different implementation behind the same token or class name.

---

## Explanation

The consumer injects the abstract token and gets whichever class you configured, so you can swap an implementation for production, testing, or a feature flag without changing the consumers.

## Example

```text
abstract class Logger { abstract log(msg: string): void; }
class ConsoleLogger extends Logger { log(msg: string) { console.log(msg); } }
class SilentLogger extends Logger { log(msg: string) {} }

providers: [{ provide: Logger, useClass: environment.prod ? SilentLogger : ConsoleLogger }]

// anywhere: private logger = inject(Logger);   // gets the configured class
```

## When to use it

Use it to replace one implementation with another, especially in tests or environment-specific code.

topics.title: What is useValue in Angular providers?
topics.body:
## Know it

`useValue` provides a ready-made value for a token: an object, a string, a number, or a configuration. Angular does not create anything; it hands out exactly that value.

---

## Explanation

It is the simplest provider and is common with an `InjectionToken` for configuration. In tests it is used to supply a fake object quickly.

## Example

```text
const API_URL = new InjectionToken<string>('API_URL');

providers: [{ provide: API_URL, useValue: 'https://api.example.com' }]

// anywhere: private apiUrl = inject(API_URL);   // 'https://api.example.com'
```

## When to use it

Use it for constants, configuration values, and test doubles.

topics.title: What is useFactory in Angular providers?
topics.body:
## Know it

`useFactory` provides a value by calling a function that you write. The function can contain logic and can receive other dependencies through `deps` or `inject()`.

---

## Explanation

It is the flexible option when the value depends on runtime conditions or needs other services to be built, for example choosing an implementation after reading configuration.

## Example

```text
const STORAGE = new InjectionToken<Storage>('STORAGE');

providers: [{
  provide: STORAGE,
  useFactory: () => environment.persist ? localStorage : sessionStorage
}]

// with dependencies
{ provide: ReportService, useFactory: (http: HttpClient, cfg: Config) => new ReportService(http, cfg.url), deps: [HttpClient, Config] }
```

## When to use it

Use it when the provided value must be created with custom logic or depends on other services.

topics.title: What is the difference between useClass, useValue, and useFactory?
topics.body:
## Know it

`useClass` provides an instance of a class, `useValue` provides an existing value, and `useFactory` calls a factory function to create a dependency, optionally using injected dependencies.

topics.title: What is an HTTP interceptor in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

An HTTP interceptor can inspect or modify outgoing HTTP requests and incoming responses. Common uses include adding authentication headers, logging, centralized error handling, and request activity indicators.

topics.title: What is a route guard in Angular?
What is the difference between a route guard and an HTTP interceptor?
topics.body:
## Know it

A route guard controls whether navigation is allowed. An HTTP interceptor handles HTTP request/response behavior. A guard is not a replacement for backend authorization; the server must enforce access rules.

topics.title: What is lazy loading in Angular routing?
topics.body:
## Know it

Lazy loading loads a route's code when that route is needed instead of including all route code in the initial bundle. It can reduce initial loading work for larger applications.

topics.title: What are template-driven forms in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Template-driven forms are defined mostly in the HTML template using directives such as `ngModel` and `ngForm`. Angular creates the form model for you behind the scenes.

---

## Explanation

They are quick to write for simple forms and need little TypeScript. Because the logic lives in the template, they are harder to test and to build dynamically, and validation rules are less explicit.

## Example

```text
<form #f="ngForm" (ngSubmit)="save(f.value)">
  <input name="email" [(ngModel)]="email" required email>
  <button [disabled]="f.invalid">Save</button>
</form>
```

## When to use it

Use them for small, simple forms such as a login or contact form.

topics.title: What are reactive forms in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Reactive forms are defined explicitly in the component class with `FormGroup`, `FormControl`, and `FormArray`. The template just binds to that model.

---

## Explanation

Because the form model is code, it is easy to build dynamic forms, add validators, react to `valueChanges`, and unit test. They scale better for large forms and cross-field validation.

## Example

```text
form = new FormGroup({
  email: new FormControl('', [Validators.required, Validators.email]),
  age: new FormControl(18, Validators.min(18))
});

<form [formGroup]="form" (ngSubmit)="save(form.value)">
  <input formControlName="email">
</form>
```

## When to use it

Use them for complex or dynamic forms, and whenever you need clear validation logic and good testability.

topics.title: What is the difference between template-driven and reactive forms?
topics.body:
## Know it

Template-driven forms rely more on directives in the template and suit simpler forms. Reactive forms define the form model in TypeScript, making complex validation and dynamic forms easier to manage and test.

topics.title: What does setValue() do in Angular forms?
topics.body:
## Know it

`setValue()` sets the value of a whole `FormGroup` or `FormArray`. You must provide a value for every control, otherwise Angular throws an error.

---

## Explanation

Because it is strict, it catches mistakes such as a missing or misspelled control name. It is a good choice when you have the complete data and want the compiler and runtime to confirm the shape matches.

## Example

```text
form = new FormGroup({ name: new FormControl(''), city: new FormControl('') });

form.setValue({ name: 'Aniket', city: 'Pune' });   // OK, all controls provided
form.setValue({ name: 'Aniket' });                 // Error: missing control 'city'
```

## When to use it

Use it when you are filling the entire form with a complete object.

topics.title: What does patchValue() do in Angular forms?
topics.body:
## Know it

`patchValue()` updates only the controls you provide and leaves the others unchanged. Missing controls do not cause an error.

---

## Explanation
