It is convenient for partial updates, such as filling in a few fields from a server response or resetting one section. Be careful: a misspelled property name is silently ignored.

## Example

```text
form = new FormGroup({ name: new FormControl('A'), city: new FormControl('B') });

form.patchValue({ name: 'Aniket' });   // only name changes
console.log(form.value);               // { name: 'Aniket', city: 'B' }
```

## When to use it

Use it when you only want to change some fields of a form.

topics.title: What is the difference between setValue() and patchValue() in Angular forms?
topics.body:
## Know it

`setValue()` requires a value for the full form structure. `patchValue()` updates only the controls supplied. Both update form values programmatically, with different strictness.

topics.title: What is trackBy in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `trackBy` is an option of the older `*ngFor` directive. It is a function that returns a unique identifier for each item, so Angular can reuse existing DOM elements when the list changes. --- ## Explanation Without it, if you replace the array with new objects, Angular destroys and recreates every row, which is slow and loses focus or scroll state. With a stable id, Angular only updates the rows that really changed. ## Example ```text trackById(index: number, user: { id: number }) { return user.id; }
  • {{ user.name }}
    • ``` ## When to use it Use it with `*ngFor` on lists that are reloaded or reordered, especially long ones.

topics.title: What is track in Angular's @for loop?
What is the difference between trackBy and track in Angular loops?
topics.body:
## Know it

Tracking lets Angular identify list items across updates and reuse DOM nodes efficiently. Modern `@for` uses a `track` expression; `trackBy` is used with `*ngFor`.

topics.title: What is the purpose of async pipe in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

The `async` pipe subscribes to an Observable or reads a Promise in the template, exposes the latest value, and manages subscription cleanup when the view is destroyed.

topics.title: What is content projection in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Content projection lets a component render content supplied between its opening and closing tags, typically using `ng-content`. It supports reusable wrappers, panels, and layout components.

topics.title: What is a directive in Angular?
What is the difference between a directive and a component?
topics.body:
## Know it

A component is a directive with its own template. Attribute and structural directives change an existing element's behavior or the rendered structure.

topics.title: What is a pure pipe in Angular?
What is an impure pipe in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it An impure pipe is declared with `pure: false` and runs on every change detection cycle, not only when its input changes. Angular's built-in `async` pipe is impure. --- ## Explanation It notices in-place changes such as items pushed into an array, but because it runs so often it can hurt performance badly if the work is heavy. Prefer a pure pipe with immutable data, or a `computed` signal. ## Example ```text @Pipe({ name: 'activeOnly', pure: false, standalone: true }) export class ActiveOnlyPipe implements PipeTransform { transform(users: { active: boolean }[]) { return users.filter(u => u.active); // re-runs on every check } }
  • {{ u.name }}
    • ``` ## When to use it Use it only when a pure pipe cannot work, and keep its logic very light.

topics.title: What is the difference between pure and impure pipes?
topics.body:
## Know it

A pure pipe runs when Angular detects a change to its input value or reference. An impure pipe can run during every change-detection cycle and may be more expensive, so it should be used carefully.

topics.title: What is an Observable in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

An Observable represents a stream that can emit values over time, then complete or error. Angular's `HttpClient` and reactive-form `valueChanges` commonly use Observables.

topics.title: What is a subscription in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

A subscription is the object you get back when you call `subscribe()` on an Observable. It represents one running connection to the stream, and you use it to stop listening with `unsubscribe()`.

---

## Explanation

An Observable by itself does nothing until someone subscribes. Each subscription starts its own run and can be cancelled on its own. Forgetting to unsubscribe from long-lived streams such as `interval`, `valueChanges`, or a `Subject` causes memory leaks.

## Example

```ts
const source$ = interval(100);
const subscription = source$.subscribe(n => console.log('tick', n));
await sleep(350);
subscription.unsubscribe();            // stop listening
console.log('closed:', subscription.closed);   // true
// printed: tick 0, tick 1, tick 2, closed: true
```

## When to use it

Keep the subscription, or use `takeUntilDestroyed` / the `async` pipe, whenever a stream does not complete by itself.

topics.title: What is the difference between an Observable and a subscription?
topics.body:
## Know it

An Observable defines the stream and how values can be produced. A subscription represents an active execution/listener and provides control such as `unsubscribe()`.

topics.title: What is a cold Observable in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

A cold Observable starts a fresh, independent execution for every subscriber. The work only begins when someone subscribes, and each subscriber gets all the values from the start.

---

## Explanation

`HttpClient` requests, `of()`, `from()`, `interval()`, and `timer()` are cold. Subscribing to an HTTP Observable twice sends two requests, which is why `shareReplay()` is used to share one result.

## Example

```ts
let executions = 0;
const cold$ = defer(() => { executions++; return of('data'); });
cold$.subscribe();
cold$.subscribe();
console.log('executions:', executions);   // 2, one per subscriber
```

## When to use it

Cold is the normal behavior. Use it when each subscriber should get its own run, such as one HTTP call per subscription.

topics.title: What is a hot Observable in RxJS?
What is the difference between cold and hot Observables?
topics.body:
## Know it

A cold Observable commonly starts a separate execution for each subscriber. A hot Observable emits independently of a particular subscriber, so multiple subscribers may observe a shared source.

topics.title: What is a Subject in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `Subject` is both an Observable and an Observer: you can subscribe to it and also push values into it with `next()`. It multicasts each value to all current subscribers.

---

## Explanation

A plain `Subject` has no memory and no initial value. Anyone who subscribes after a value was emitted never sees that value. It is ideal for events, such as "user logged out" or "item saved".

## Example

```ts
const subject = new Subject<string>();
subject.next('missed');                          // nobody is listening yet
subject.subscribe(v => console.log('received', v));
subject.next('seen');
// printed: received seen
```

## When to use it

Use it as an event bus, to signal that something happened.

topics.title: What is a BehaviorSubject in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `BehaviorSubject` is a Subject that always holds a current value. It needs an initial value, and every new subscriber immediately receives the latest value.

---

## Explanation

You can read the latest value synchronously with `.value`. This makes it a simple tool for shared state such as the logged-in user or the selected filter. Do not expose the subject itself; expose `asObservable()`.

## Example

```ts
const user$ = new BehaviorSubject('guest');
user$.subscribe(v => console.log('A:', v));      // A: guest   (immediately)
user$.next('Aniket');                            // A: Aniket
user$.subscribe(v => console.log('B:', v));      // B: Aniket  (latest value at once)
console.log('current:', user$.value);            // current: Aniket
```

## When to use it

Use it for state that always has a current value and that late subscribers must see right away.

topics.title: What is the difference between Subject and BehaviorSubject?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `Subject` multicasts values to current subscribers but does not replay a previous value to new subscribers. A `BehaviorSubject` requires an initial value and immediately emits its latest value to a new subscriber.

topics.title: What is a ReplaySubject in RxJS?
What is the difference between ReplaySubject and BehaviorSubject?
topics.body:
## Know it

`BehaviorSubject` stores and replays the latest value and requires an initial value. `ReplaySubject` can replay a configured buffer of previous values and does not require an initial value.

topics.title: What does map() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

RxJS `map()` transforms each emitted value and emits the transformed value. It does not automatically subscribe to an inner Observable.

topics.title: What does tap() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`tap()` performs side effects such as logging or updating a loading indicator without changing the emitted value. It is not intended for transforming data.

topics.title: What is the difference between RxJS map() and Array map()?
topics.body:
## Know it

Array `map()` transforms array elements immediately and returns an array. RxJS `map()` transforms each value emitted by an Observable over time and returns another Observable.

topics.title: What does filter() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

RxJS `filter()` allows only values that satisfy a condition to pass through the stream. It filters emissions, not the contents of an emitted array unless the predicate is written to do that.

topics.title: What does take() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`take(n)` emits only the first `n` values and then completes. It is useful when only a fixed number of emissions are needed.

topics.title: What does skip() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`skip(n)` ignores the first `n` values of a stream and passes along everything after them. The stream still completes normally.

---

## Explanation

It is the opposite idea of `take(n)`. A common use is `skip(1)` on a `BehaviorSubject`, to ignore its initial current value and react only to later changes.

## Example

```ts
of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).pipe(skip(2)).subscribe(v => console.log(v));
// 3, 4, 5

const state$ = new BehaviorSubject('initial');
state$.pipe(skip(1)).subscribe(v => console.log('changed to', v));
state$.next('A');   // changed to A
```

## When to use it

Use it to ignore the first emissions, especially the starting value of a `BehaviorSubject`.

topics.title: What is the difference between take() and skip() in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`take(n)` keeps the first `n` emissions and then completes. `skip(n)` ignores the first `n` emissions and passes subsequent values.

topics.title: What does debounceTime() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`debounceTime()` waits for a pause in emissions and then emits the most recent value. It is often used with search inputs to reduce requests while a user is typing.

topics.title: What does distinctUntilChanged() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`distinctUntilChanged()` suppresses consecutive emissions that compare equal using its comparator. It is commonly used after normalizing a search string to avoid duplicate requests.

topics.title: What does switchMap do in RxJS?
What does mergeMap do in RxJS?
What is the difference between switchMap and mergeMap?
topics.body:
## Know it

`switchMap` switches to the newest inner Observable and unsubscribes from the previous inner subscription. `mergeMap` allows multiple inner Observables to run concurrently, so results may arrive out of order.

topics.title: What does concatMap do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`concatMap` maps each value to an inner Observable and runs them one after another, in order. The next one starts only when the previous one completes.

---

## Explanation

The order of the results always matches the order of the inputs, which makes it safe for operations that must not overlap. The cost is time: the total time is the sum of all the tasks.

## Example

```ts
const t0 = Date.now();
const save = (n: number) => of('saved ' + n).pipe(delay(100));
from([1, 2, 3]).pipe(concatMap(save)).subscribe(v =>
  console.log(v, 'after', Math.round((Date.now() - t0) / 100) * 100, 'ms'));
// saved 1 after 100 ms, saved 2 after 200 ms, saved 3 after 300 ms
```

## When to use it

Use it when order matters, for example saving changes in the order the user made them.

topics.title: What is the difference between concatMap and mergeMap?
topics.body:
## Know it

`concatMap` processes inner Observables sequentially, waiting for one to complete before starting the next. `mergeMap` allows concurrent inner work.

topics.title: What does exhaustMap do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`exhaustMap` maps a value to an inner Observable and ignores every new value that arrives while that inner Observable is still running.

---

## Explanation

While one request is in progress, extra triggers are dropped, not queued and not cancelling. This prevents duplicate requests from a user who clicks repeatedly. Once the inner Observable completes, the next value is accepted again.

## Example

```ts
let requests = 0;
const save = () => { requests++; return of('saved').pipe(delay(200)); };
const clicks$ = from([1, 2, 3]).pipe(concatMap(x => of(x).pipe(delay(50))));  // 3 quick clicks
clicks$.pipe(exhaustMap(save)).subscribe(v => console.log(v));
await sleep(500);
console.log('requests sent:', requests);   // 1
```

## When to use it

Use it for submit and login buttons, so repeated clicks do not send duplicate requests.

topics.title: What is the difference between exhaustMap and switchMap?
topics.body:
## Know it

`exhaustMap` ignores new source emissions while the current inner Observable is active. `switchMap` cancels the previous inner subscription and switches to the newest one.

topics.title: What does forkJoin() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`forkJoin()` waits for all input Observables to complete, then emits their last values together. It is useful for combining finite HTTP requests that must all finish.

topics.title: What does combineLatest() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`combineLatest` combines several Observables and emits an array of their latest values every time any of them emits, once each source has emitted at least once.

---

## Explanation

It never emits until all sources have produced a first value, and it keeps emitting as long as the sources keep emitting. It completes only when all sources complete. It is ideal for things that change over time, like several filter values.

## Example

```ts
const a$ = interval(100).pipe(take(3));   // 0, 1, 2
const b$ = interval(150).pipe(take(2));   // 0, 1
combineLatest([a$, b$]).subscribe(v => console.log(JSON.stringify(v)));
// [0,0] [1,0] [2,0] [2,1]   an array each time either source changes
```

## When to use it

Use it when a result depends on several values that keep changing, such as search text plus the selected category plus a date range.

topics.title: What is the difference between forkJoin() and combineLatest()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`forkJoin()` emits once after all sources complete, using their last values. `combineLatest()` emits whenever a source changes after every source has emitted at least once.

topics.title: What does catchError() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`catchError()` handles an Observable error and returns a replacement Observable, such as a fallback value or another request. The replacement choice determines whether the stream continues or completes.

topics.title: What does finalize() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`finalize()` runs a callback when the Observable terminates or is unsubscribed. It is useful for cleanup such as resetting a loading flag.

topics.title: What does firstValueFrom() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`firstValueFrom` converts an Observable into a Promise that resolves with the first value the Observable emits, and then unsubscribes automatically.

---

## Explanation

It lets you use `await` with an Observable, for example `await firstValueFrom(http.get(...))`. If the Observable completes without emitting, the Promise rejects with an `EmptyError` unless you pass a `defaultValue`. It replaces the deprecated `toPromise()`.

## Example

```ts
const first = await firstValueFrom(of(1, 2, 3));
console.log(first);                                   // 1
console.log(await firstValueFrom(EMPTY, { defaultValue: 'none' })); // 'none'
```

## When to use it

Use it when you need exactly one value from a stream, typically a single HTTP response, inside `async` code.

topics.title: What does lastValueFrom() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`lastValueFrom` converts an Observable into a Promise that resolves with the last value emitted, but only after the Observable completes.

---

## Explanation

Because it must wait for completion, it never resolves for streams that do not complete, like a `BehaviorSubject` or `interval`, so your `await` hangs forever. It is useful for streams that emit progress and then a final result.

## Example

```ts
const last = await lastValueFrom(of(1, 2, 3));
console.log(last);   // 3

// const hangs = await lastValueFrom(interval(1000));   // never finishes!
console.log(await lastValueFrom(interval(50).pipe(take(4))));   // 3, after take() completes it
```

## When to use it

Use it when only the final result matters and the stream is known to complete.

topics.title: What is the difference between firstValueFrom() and lastValueFrom()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`firstValueFrom()` resolves with the first emitted value and unsubscribes. `lastValueFrom()` waits for completion and resolves with the last emitted value, so it can hang if the source never completes.

topics.title: What is shareReplay() used for?
topics.body:
## Know it

`shareReplay()` shares source work among subscribers and replays a configured number of recent values. It can help cache an HTTP result, but the configuration and lifetime should be chosen carefully.

topics.title: Why is unsubscribing important in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

Unsubscribing stops an active subscription and can prevent unnecessary work or memory leaks for long-lived streams. Many Angular HTTP Observables complete automatically, while event streams and subjects may stay active.

topics.title: What does takeUntil() do in RxJS?
What is the difference between takeUntil() and take(1)?
topics.body:
## Know it

`take(1)` completes after the first value. `takeUntil(notifier$)` completes when the notifier emits, which is useful for tying a stream's lifetime to component destruction or another stop event.

topics.title: Scenario: An API response sometimes has no nested customer address. How would you prevent a runtime error?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use optional chaining for safe access and still handle the missing data intentionally. Optional chaining prevents an error for nullish intermediate values, but it does not validate the complete API response.

---

## Explanation

For example, use `response.customer?.address?.city ?? 'Not provided'` when a fallback is appropriate.

## Example

```ts
const city = response.customer?.address?.city ?? 'Not provided';
```

## When to use it

Use this when nested response fields are optional; validate the response if its shape is untrusted.

topics.title: Scenario: A search request for an older term finishes after the latest search. How would you avoid showing stale results?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use a latest-request strategy. In Angular with RxJS, `debounceTime()` and `switchMap()` are a common combination because `switchMap()` unsubscribes from the previous inner request when a newer term arrives.

---

## Explanation

The API or server may still finish processing a canceled request, but the old Observable result is no longer forwarded through that switched stream.

## Example

```ts
searchControl.valueChanges.pipe(
  debounceTime(300),
  distinctUntilChanged(),
  switchMap(term => this.api.search(term))
);
```

## When to use it

Use for autocomplete and search-as-you-type experiences.

topics.title: Scenario: A user clicks Submit several times and duplicate requests are sent. How would you prevent this?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would disable the button while the request is in progress and make the submission flow guard against repeated clicks. In RxJS, `exhaustMap()` can ignore new submit events until the active request completes. The backend should also protect against duplicate submissions where needed.

---

## Explanation

UI prevention improves experience, but server-side idempotency may be required for important transactions.

## Example

```ts
submitClicks$.pipe(exhaustMap(() => this.api.submit(this.form.value)));
```

## When to use it

Use for submit/payment-like actions where concurrent duplicate requests are undesirable.

topics.title: Scenario: You need to run three independent API requests and show the page only when all finish. What would you use?
topics.body:
## Know it

If the requests are finite Observables such as Angular HTTP calls, I would use `forkJoin()` and handle errors deliberately. It emits the final result from each source once all complete.

---

## Explanation

If one request may fail independently, I would decide whether to catch errors inside each request so the other results can still be shown.

## Example

```ts
forkJoin({
  profile: this.api.getProfile(),
  settings: this.api.getSettings(),
  alerts: this.api.getAlerts()
});
```

## When to use it

Use when all results are required together and the sources complete.

topics.title: Scenario: You must process save requests in the exact order the user created them. Which operator would you choose?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use `concatMap()` so each inner request completes before the next starts. This preserves processing order, unlike concurrent `mergeMap()` calls.

---

## Explanation

I would also consider disabling actions or showing progress if the queue could become long.

## Example

```ts
saveActions$.pipe(concatMap(item => this.api.save(item)));
```

## When to use it

Use when order matters, such as sequential updates.

topics.title: Scenario: You need to show a loading spinner for an API request even when it fails. How would you implement it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would set the loading state before the request and reset it in `finalize()`, because `finalize()` runs on completion, error, or unsubscription.

---

## Explanation

I would still use `catchError()` at an appropriate layer to display a useful error message.

## Example

```ts
this.loading = true;
this.api.load().pipe(
  finalize(() => this.loading = false)
).subscribe({
  next: data => this.data = data,
  error: () => this.errorMessage = 'Unable to load data'
});
```

## When to use it

Use for request-driven loading indicators.

topics.title: Scenario: Updating one property of an object unexpectedly changes data shown elsewhere. What could be wrong?
topics.body:
## Know it

The code may have changed a shared object reference instead of creating a copy. I would check where the object is shared and use an immutable update, including copying nested objects when those are changed.

---

## Explanation

A shallow spread copy does not isolate nested objects automatically.

## Example

```ts
const updated = { ...user, profile: { ...user.profile, city: 'Nagpur' } };
```

## When to use it

Use when state is shared between components, services, or views.

topics.title: Scenario: A function returns different results because asynchronous calls finish in different orders. How would you debug it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would identify which operations are independent and which must be ordered. Then I would use `Promise.all()` for independent work or sequential `await`/a sequential RxJS operator when order is required, and make error handling explicit.

---

## Explanation

Avoid relying on completion order unless the code explicitly coordinates it.

## When to use it

Use when results depend on multiple asynchronous operations.

topics.title: Scenario: You need to remove duplicate IDs from an API result. What would you do?
topics.body:
## Know it

For primitive IDs, I would use a `Set` to keep unique values. If I need unique objects, I would define the key used to identify duplicates and build the result around that key.

---

## Explanation

Object identity is not the same as equality by an `id` property.

## Example

```ts
const uniqueIds = [...new Set(rows.map(row => row.id))];
```

## When to use it

Use for de-duplicating IDs or other primitive values.

topics.title: Scenario: A component needs a callback but loses the expected this value. What would you check?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would check how the function is passed and invoked. A regular function's `this` depends on the call site; an arrow function captures lexical `this`. I would choose the appropriate function form or bind the method if needed.

---

## Explanation

Do not assume `this` stays attached when a method is passed as a standalone callback.

## When to use it

Use when passing class methods as callbacks.

topics.title: Scenario: An API field may be a string, a number, or null. How would you type it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would represent the actual contract with a union such as `string | number | null`, then narrow the value before using type-specific operations. I would avoid `any` because it removes useful checks.

---

## Explanation

If the backend contract can change or data is untrusted, compile-time typing should be paired with runtime validation.

topics.title: Scenario: You receive data from an API but cannot guarantee its shape. Is an interface enough?
topics.body:
## Know it

An interface describes the expected shape at compile time but does not validate incoming JSON at runtime. I would type the incoming value as `unknown` and validate or parse it before treating it as the expected model.

---

## Explanation

The `HttpClient` generic provides a compile-time type assertion; it does not inspect the actual payload.

topics.title: Scenario: Several functions accept the same object shape. How would you avoid repeating that type?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would define a reusable interface or type and use it across the functions. If a function should support different types while preserving their type information, I would consider a generic.

topics.title: Scenario: A function accepts a property name, but TypeScript allows misspelled keys. How can you restrict it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use a generic key parameter constrained by `keyof` the object type. That makes TypeScript reject keys that are not valid properties.

topics.title: Scenario: A status can only be 'pending', 'success', or 'failed'. How would you model it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use a string-literal union such as `'pending' | 'success' | 'failed'`. It limits valid values at compile time and makes conditional handling clearer.

topics.title: Scenario: TypeScript says a value may be undefined. How should you handle it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would check whether the value exists and narrow the type before accessing it, or supply a meaningful default if that fits the requirement. I would avoid using a non-null assertion unless the value's existence is guaranteed by the surrounding logic.

topics.title: Scenario: You need a reusable function that returns the same type it receives. What TypeScript feature helps?
topics.body:
## Know it

A generic type parameter preserves the relationship between the input and output types. For example, a function taking `T` can return `T` without losing its specific type.

topics.title: Scenario: A switch statement must handle every member of a union. How can you catch a missing case?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use a discriminated union and an exhaustive check with `never` in the default branch. TypeScript can then report a type error if a new union member is not handled.

topics.title: Scenario: You need a type for an update form where every field is optional. Which utility type fits?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Partial<T>` makes all properties of `T` optional. I would use it only if partial updates are actually allowed by the API contract.

topics.title: Scenario: You need only id and name from a large model. Which utility type can help?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Pick<Model, 'id' | 'name'>` creates a type containing only the selected properties. `Omit` would be appropriate if I instead needed to exclude specific fields.

topics.title: What is data binding in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it Data binding connects the component class to its template, so the view shows the current data and user actions reach the class. Angular has four forms: interpolation, property binding, event binding, and two-way binding. --- ## Explanation Data flows from the class to the view with `{{ }}` and `[property]`, from the view to the class with `(event)`, and in both directions with `[(ngModel)]`. Angular keeps the view in sync through change detection, so you rarely touch the DOM yourself. ## Example ```text

{{ title }}

``` ## When to use it Use it for everything that shows data or reacts to the user; it is the core of every Angular template.

topics.title: What is interpolation in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it Interpolation writes a value from the component into the template text using double curly braces: `{{ expression }}`. The result is always converted to a string. --- ## Explanation The expression can read properties, call simple methods, and use operators, but it cannot assign values or use `new`, `;`, or `++`. Angular re-evaluates it on each change detection pass, so keep it cheap. ## Example ```text

Hello {{ user.name }}, you have {{ items.length }} items.

Total: {{ price * quantity | currency }}

``` ## When to use it Use it to display text, numbers, and formatted values inside an element.

topics.title: What is property binding in Angular?
topics.body: ## Know it Property binding sets a DOM property or a child component input from an expression, written as `[property]="expression"`. The value keeps its real type (boolean, number, object), not just text. --- ## Explanation It binds to element properties such as `disabled`, `src`, `hidden`, and `value`, and to `@Input` properties of child components. Angular updates the property whenever the expression result changes. ## Example ```text ``` ## When to use it Use it whenever you need to set a non-text value, pass data to a child, or toggle a property such as `disabled`.

topics.title: What is the difference between interpolation and property binding?
topics.body:
## Know it Interpolation (`{{ value }}`) always produces a string, while property binding (`[prop]="value"`) passes the real value with its type. For text they look the same, but for booleans and objects they behave differently. --- ## Explanation Interpolation inside an attribute is turned into a string, so `disabled="{{ false }}"` becomes the string `"false"`, which is truthy, and the element ends up disabled. Property binding passes the boolean `false` correctly. ## Example ```text

{{ name }}

``` ## When to use it Use interpolation for text content; use property binding for booleans, objects, and any non-text value.

topics.title: What is event binding in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Event binding listens to an event and runs a template statement or method when it happens, written as `(event)="handler()"`. It sends information from the view to the class.

---

## Explanation

You can listen to DOM events like `click` and `keyup`, or to a child component's `@Output`. The special `$event` variable holds the event data, so you can pass it to the handler. Keep handlers short and move logic into the class.

## Example

```text
<button (click)="save()">Save</button>
<input (keyup.enter)="search($event.target.value)">
<app-save-button (saved)="onSaved($event)"></app-save-button>
```

## When to use it

Use it to react to clicks, typing, form submission, and events emitted by child components.

topics.title: What is two-way binding in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it Two-way binding keeps a template element and a class property in sync in both directions, using the "banana in a box" syntax `[(property)]`. It is a shortcut for a property binding plus an event binding. --- ## Explanation `[(ngModel)]="name"` is the same as `[ngModel]="name" (ngModelChange)="name = $event"`. It needs `FormsModule` for `ngModel`. For your own components, create an `@Input() value` and an `@Output() valueChange` pair, or use the `model()` signal. ## Example ```text

You typed: {{ name }}

``` ## When to use it Use it for simple form inputs; for larger forms prefer reactive forms, which are easier to validate and test.

topics.title: What is a template reference variable in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A template reference variable is a name starting with `#` that points to a DOM element, a component, or a directive inside the same template. You can use it anywhere in that template.

---

## Explanation

On a plain element it refers to the element; on a component it refers to the component instance; with `exportAs`, such as `#f="ngForm"`, it refers to that directive. It lets you read values or call methods without extra properties in the class.

## Example

```text
<input #nameBox placeholder="Name">
<button (click)="greet(nameBox.value)">Greet</button>

<form #f="ngForm"> ... </form>
<button [disabled]="f.invalid">Submit</button>
```

## When to use it

Use it for quick access to an element's value or a child component's API from the template.

topics.title: What is the @if block in Angular?
What is the *ngIf directive in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `*ngIf` is the older structural directive that adds an element to the page when its condition is true and removes it when false. It is provided by `NgIf` (CommonModule) and must be imported. --- ## Explanation The element is really removed from the DOM and its component is destroyed, unlike `[hidden]`, which only hides it. The else part needs a separate `` and a reference, which is more verbose than `@if`. ## Example ```text

Welcome {{ user.name }}

Please sign in

 ``` ## When to use it You will meet it in existing code; in new code use `@if`.

topics.title: What is the difference between *ngIf and @if?
topics.body:
## Know it `@if` is the new built-in control flow block (Angular 17+), while `*ngIf` is the older directive. Both show or remove content based on a condition, but `@if` is simpler and faster. --- ## Explanation `@if` needs no import, has a readable `@else` / `@else if` syntax, and is compiled into the template instead of being a directive. `*ngIf` needs `NgIf` imported and an `ng-template` for else. `*ngIf` is being replaced and has a migration schematic. ## Example ```text
Admin tools
User tools @if (isAdmin) {
Admin tools
} @else {
User tools
} ``` ## When to use it Use `@if` in new code and migrate old templates with `ng generate @angular/core:control-flow`.

What is ViewEncapsulation in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `ViewEncapsulation` controls whether a component's CSS applies only to that component or leaks to the rest of the app. The modes are `Emulated` (default), `None`, and `ShadowDom`. --- ## Explanation With `Emulated`, Angular adds unique attributes (like `_ngcontent-abc`) so styles stay inside the component. With `None`, the styles become global. With `ShadowDom`, the browser's native shadow DOM isolates the styles. Styles from the parent do not reach an encapsulated child. ## Example ```text @Component({ selector: 'app-card', template: `

Hi

`, styles: ['.title { color: teal; }'], encapsulation: ViewEncapsulation.Emulated // None | ShadowDom }) export class CardComponent {} ``` ## When to use it Keep the default for almost everything; use `None` only for deliberately global styles, and `ShadowDom` for web-component-style isolation.

What is the injector hierarchy in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Angular has a tree of injectors. When something asks for a dependency, Angular looks first in the component's own injector, then in its parent components, and finally in the root (environment) injector, using the first provider it finds.

---

## Explanation

There are two kinds: node (element) injectors that follow the component tree, and environment injectors (root, plus lazy-loaded routes). This is why a service in a component's `providers` is private to that subtree, and one with `providedIn: 'root'` is shared by everyone.

## Example

```text
root injector            AuthService (singleton)
 └─ AppComponent
     └─ ListComponent    providers: [FilterState]   <- own instance
         └─ ItemComponent   inject(FilterState)     <- finds the parent's instance
                            inject(AuthService)     <- found in root
```

## When to use it

Know it to decide where to provide a service: root for shared singletons, a component for per-instance state.

topics.title: What is the inject() function in Angular?
What is constructor injection in Angular?

What are multi providers in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A multi provider registers several values under one token with `multi: true`, so injecting the token gives you an array of all of them instead of just one.

---

## Explanation

Angular uses this for extension points such as `NG_VALIDATORS`, `APP_INITIALIZER`, and (historically) `HTTP_INTERCEPTORS`. Each `provide` with the same token adds an item to the array, in order.

## Example

```text
export const PLUGIN = new InjectionToken<string[]>('PLUGIN');

providers: [
  { provide: PLUGIN, useValue: 'logger', multi: true },
  { provide: PLUGIN, useValue: 'analytics', multi: true }
]

const plugins = inject(PLUGIN);   // ['logger', 'analytics']
```

## When to use it

Use it when many independent parts should contribute to one list, such as plugins or validators.

topics.title: What are viewProviders in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`viewProviders` registers a service that is available only to the component's own view (its template children), not to content projected into it through `<ng-content>`.

---

## Explanation

It narrows who can see a provider. Content children that are projected into the component cannot inject a service listed in `viewProviders`, which protects it from outside code.

## Example

```text
@Component({
  selector: 'app-secure-box',
  viewProviders: [SecretService],          // only the template children can use it
  template: `<app-inner></app-inner><ng-content></ng-content>`
})
export class SecureBoxComponent {}
```

## When to use it

Use it rarely, when a service must be hidden from projected content.

topics.title: What is the difference between providers and viewProviders?
What are @Optional, @Self, @SkipSelf, and @Host in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

These are resolution modifiers that change how Angular looks up a dependency: `@Optional` allows it to be missing, `@Self` looks only in the current injector, `@SkipSelf` starts at the parent, and `@Host` stops at the host component.

---

## Explanation

Without them, a missing provider throws an error and the lookup climbs the whole tree. With `inject()` they are passed as options: `inject(Token, { optional: true, self: true, skipSelf: true, host: true })`.

## Example

```text
constructor(
  @Optional() private logger: Logger | null,     // no error if not provided
  @SkipSelf() private parent: ThemeService       // use the parent's instance, not my own
) {}

private cfg = inject(CONFIG, { optional: true });   // function style
```

## When to use it

Use `@Optional` for optional features, and `@SkipSelf` / `@Self` for nested services that must find the right level.

topics.title: What are lifecycle hooks in Angular?
What is ngDoCheck in Angular?
What is the difference between ngOnChanges and ngDoCheck?
topics.body:
## Know it

`ngOnChanges` runs only when an input reference changes. `ngDoCheck` runs on every change detection pass and lets you detect changes manually.

---

## Explanation

If a parent pushes an item into an array it passes down, the reference is the same, so `ngOnChanges` does not fire, but `ngDoCheck` does run and can compare the contents.

## Example

```text
// parent: this.list.push('x');   (same array reference)
ngOnChanges() { console.log('not called'); }
ngDoCheck()   { console.log('called - compare contents here'); }
```

## When to use it

Prefer `ngOnChanges` (cheap, targeted); use `ngDoCheck` only for mutations inside objects or arrays.

topics.title: What is ngAfterContentInit in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`ngAfterContentInit` runs once after Angular has put the projected content (from `<ng-content>`) into the component. `@ContentChild` is ready here.

---

## Explanation

It comes before `ngAfterViewInit`, because projected content is created before the component's own view is finished. `ngAfterContentChecked` is the same idea but runs after every check.

## Example

```text
@ContentChild('title') title!: ElementRef;
ngAfterContentInit() { console.log(this.title.nativeElement.textContent); }
```

## When to use it

Use it in wrapper components such as tabs or cards that need to inspect what the parent passes in.

topics.title: What is ngOnDestroy in Angular?
What is the Default change detection strategy?
topics.body:
## Know it

With the Default strategy, Angular checks the component on every change detection pass, even if none of its inputs changed.

---

## Explanation

It is simple and always correct, because anything that changes is picked up. In large apps, though, checking the whole tree each time wastes work.

## Example

```text
@Component({
  selector: 'app-card',
  template: `{{ user.name }}`
  // changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.Default   (this is the default)
})
```

## When to use it

Fine for small apps and quick prototypes; switch to OnPush when the app grows.

topics.title: What is the OnPush change detection strategy?
topics.body:
## Know it

With OnPush, Angular checks a component only when an input reference changes, an event fires inside it, an `async` pipe emits, a signal it reads changes, or you mark it manually.

---

## Explanation

OnPush works on reference changes, not mutation. If you change a property inside an object that was passed in, the component will not update. You replace the object with a new copy instead.

## Example

```text
@Component({
  selector: 'app-user',
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `{{ user.name }}`
})
export class UserComponent { @Input() user!: User; }

// parent
this.user.name = 'Ram';              // NOT detected by the child
this.user = { ...this.user, name: 'Ram' };   // detected: new reference
```

## When to use it

Use it for almost every component in a real app, together with immutable updates and the async pipe.

topics.title: What is the difference between Default and OnPush?
topics.body:
## Know it

Default checks the component on every pass. OnPush checks it only when its inputs change by reference, an event or async pipe fires, a signal changes, or it is marked dirty.

---

## Explanation

OnPush skips whole parts of the tree, so it is faster, but you must update data immutably. Default is more forgiving but does more work.

## Example

```text
// Default: mutation works
this.user.name = 'Ram';       // view updates

// OnPush: mutation is ignored, a new object works
this.user = { ...this.user, name: 'Ram' };
```

## When to use it

Choose OnPush for performance in anything beyond a small app.

topics.title: What is Zone.js in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Zone.js is a library that patches async browser APIs (events, timers, HTTP) so Angular knows when an async task finishes and can run change detection.

---

## Explanation

It wraps `setTimeout`, promises, and DOM events. When one of them completes, Zone.js tells Angular, and Angular updates the view. That is why you do not have to refresh the screen by hand.

## Example

```text
setTimeout(() => {
  this.message = 'Loaded';     // Angular refreshes the view automatically
}, 1000);
```

## When to use it

You rarely use it directly; knowing it explains why the UI updates after async work.

topics.title: What is NgZone in Angular?
What is the difference between runOutsideAngular and ngZone.run?
What is zoneless Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Zoneless Angular runs without Zone.js. Change detection is triggered by signals, `markForCheck`, events, and the async pipe, not by every async task.

---

## Explanation

Without Zone.js, the bundle is smaller and fewer checks run. State must be held in signals (or OnPush-friendly code) so Angular knows what to update.

## Example

```text
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, {
  providers: [provideZonelessChangeDetection()]
});

count = signal(0);
inc() { this.count.update(c => c + 1); }   // the view updates because a signal changed
```

## When to use it

Use it in new apps built with signals and OnPush-style code.

topics.title: What is the difference between detectChanges and markForCheck?
What is trackBy and why use it?
How do you avoid memory leaks in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A memory leak happens when a component is gone but its subscriptions, timers, or listeners keep running. You avoid it by cleaning up when the component is destroyed.

---

## Explanation

The main tools are: the `async` pipe (auto cleanup), `takeUntilDestroyed()` (Angular 16+), the `takeUntil(destroy$)` pattern, manual `unsubscribe()` in `ngOnDestroy`, and `toSignal()` (no manual subscription).

## Example

```text
private destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef);

ngOnInit() {
  this.api.getData()
    .pipe(takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef))
    .subscribe(d => this.data = d);
}

// template alternative: <li *ngFor="let u of users$ | async">
```

## When to use it

Do it for every long-living subscription, such as `valueChanges`, `interval`, sockets, and route params.

topics.title: How do you check Angular app performance?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use Angular DevTools, the Chrome Performance and Network tabs, Lighthouse, and a bundle analyzer to find slow rendering, large bundles, and wasteful API calls.

---

## Explanation

Angular DevTools shows which components re-render and how often. The Performance tab shows long tasks. The Network tab shows slow or duplicate API calls. A bundle analyzer shows which libraries are large.

## Example

```text
ng build --configuration production
npx source-map-explorer dist/**/*.js     // see what makes the bundle big

// Chrome: F12 -> Performance -> Record -> use the app -> Stop
// Chrome: F12 -> Lighthouse -> Analyze page load
```

## When to use it

Measure before optimizing, so you fix the real bottleneck.

topics.title: How do you optimize Angular performance?
What is tree shaking in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Tree shaking removes code you never use from the final bundle, so the app downloads less.

---

## Explanation

It works because the build analyzes ES module imports. Code that is never imported is dropped. `providedIn: 'root'` services that are never injected are also removed.

## Example

```text
import { debounceTime } from 'rxjs';   // only this operator ends up in the bundle
// a service that nothing injects -> removed from the production build
```

## When to use it

It is automatic in production builds; help it by importing only what you need.

topics.title: What is the difference between JIT and AOT compilation?
topics.body:
## Know it

JIT compiles templates in the browser while the app runs. AOT compiles them during the build, so the browser receives ready-to-run JavaScript.

---

## Explanation

AOT gives faster startup, smaller bundles, and catches template errors at build time. JIT is slower to start and ships the compiler to the browser. Modern Angular uses AOT by default, in development too.

## Example

```text
ng build                         // AOT by default
ng build --configuration production
// a typo in a template binding fails the build with AOT, instead of failing in the browser
```

## When to use it

Always use AOT for production.

topics.title: What is the @defer block in Angular?
What is Angular routing?
topics.body: ## Know it Routing maps URLs to components so a single page app can show different views without reloading the page. --- ## Explanation Routes are defined in an array of `{ path, component }` objects, and `` shows the matching component. You navigate with `routerLink` or the `Router` service. ## Example ```text export const routes: Routes = [ { path: '', redirectTo: 'home', pathMatch: 'full' }, { path: 'home', component: HomeComponent }, { path: 'users/:id', component: UserComponent }, { path: '**', component: NotFoundComponent } ]; Home ``` ## When to use it Every multi-page Angular app uses it.

topics.title: What is lazy loading in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Lazy loading downloads a route's code only when the user visits that route, instead of at startup.

---

## Explanation

It makes the first load smaller and faster. You use `loadComponent` for one standalone component or `loadChildren` for a group of routes.

## Example

```text
{
  path: 'admin',
  loadChildren: () => import('./admin/admin.routes').then(m => m.ADMIN_ROUTES)
},
{
  path: 'reports',
  loadComponent: () => import('./reports/reports.component').then(m => m.ReportsComponent)
}
```

## When to use it

Use it for feature areas that not every user opens.

topics.title: What is the difference between lazy loading, eager loading, and preloading?
topics.body:
## Know it

Eager loading loads everything at startup. Lazy loading loads a route when it is first visited. Preloading loads lazy routes in the background after the app has started.

---

## Explanation

Eager is simple but slow to start. Lazy gives a fast start but a small delay on the first visit. Preloading removes that delay by fetching lazy routes while the user is idle.

## Example

```text
provideRouter(routes, withPreloading(PreloadAllModules))   // preload lazy routes after startup

{ path: 'home', component: HomeComponent }                      // eager
{ path: 'admin', loadChildren: () => import('./admin/routes') } // lazy
```

## When to use it

Lazy for large feature areas; preloading for routes users are likely to open next.

topics.title: What are route guards in Angular?
What is CanActivate in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`CanActivate` decides whether a user may enter a route. If it returns false, navigation is blocked, or you can return a redirect.

---

## Explanation

It runs after the route matches but before the component is created. It is the usual login guard.

## Example

```text
export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = (route, state) =>
  inject(AuthService).isLoggedIn() || inject(Router).createUrlTree(['/login']);
```

## When to use it

Use it to protect a page for logged-in users.

topics.title: What is CanActivateChild in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`CanActivateChild` protects all child routes of a parent route with one guard.

---

## Explanation

Instead of adding `canActivate` to every child, you add `canActivateChild` once on the parent.

## Example

```text
{
  path: 'admin',
  canActivateChild: [adminGuard],
  children: [
    { path: 'users', component: UsersComponent },
    { path: 'reports', component: ReportsComponent }
  ]
}
```

## When to use it

Use it for a whole section such as `/admin/...`.

topics.title: What is CanMatch in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`CanMatch` decides whether a route should match at all, before Angular loads it. It is the modern replacement for `CanLoad`.

---

## Explanation

If it returns false, Angular tries the next route with the same path. That allows two different components for the same URL depending on the role, and it prevents lazy code from being downloaded for users who cannot use it.

## Example

```text
export const adminMatch: CanMatchFn = () => inject(AuthService).isAdmin();

{ path: 'home', canMatch: [adminMatch], component: AdminHomeComponent },
{ path: 'home', component: UserHomeComponent }
```

## When to use it

Use it for role-based lazy routes or feature flags.

topics.title: What is the difference between CanActivate and CanMatch?
topics.body:
## Know it

`CanMatch` runs before the route is matched and before lazy code is loaded. `CanActivate` runs after the route matched, and the code may already be downloaded.

---

## Explanation

With `CanActivate`, a blocked user may still have downloaded the lazy bundle. With `CanMatch`, the route is treated as if it did not exist, so nothing is loaded.

## Example

```text
{ path: 'admin', loadChildren: ..., canMatch: [adminGuard] }     // bundle not downloaded if blocked
{ path: 'admin', loadChildren: ..., canActivate: [adminGuard] }  // bundle may already be downloaded
```

## When to use it

Use `CanMatch` for lazy-loaded protected areas; `CanActivate` for simple checks.

topics.title: What is CanDeactivate in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`CanDeactivate` decides whether a user may leave the current page. It is commonly used to warn about unsaved changes.

---

## Explanation

The guard receives the component instance, so it can ask the component whether the form is dirty, and then show a confirm dialog.

## Example

```text
export const unsavedGuard: CanDeactivateFn<EditComponent> = (component) =>
  component.form.dirty ? confirm('Leave without saving?') : true;

{ path: 'edit', component: EditComponent, canDeactivate: [unsavedGuard] }
```

## When to use it

Use it for edit forms where losing data would hurt.

topics.title: What is a Resolver in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A resolver loads the data a route needs before the route opens, so the component starts with its data already there.

---

## Explanation

Angular waits for the resolver to finish. The result is available in `route.data`. If it fails, you can redirect instead of showing an empty page.

## Example

```text
export const userResolver: ResolveFn<User> = (route) =>
  inject(UserService).getUser(route.paramMap.get('id')!);

{ path: 'user/:id', component: UserComponent, resolve: { user: userResolver } }

// component
this.route.data.subscribe(d => this.user = d['user']);
```

## When to use it

Use it when a page is useless without its data and you want to avoid a half-empty screen.

topics.title: How do route parameters and query parameters differ?
topics.body:
## Know it

Route parameters are part of the path (`/users/5`) and identify a resource. Query parameters come after `?` (`/users?page=2&role=admin`) and are optional, used for filters, paging, and sorting.

---

## Explanation

Read route params with `paramMap`, and query params with `queryParamMap`. Both are observables, because the component is reused when only the parameter changes.

## Example

```text
this.router.navigate(['/users', 5], { queryParams: { tab: 'info' } });   // /users/5?tab=info

this.route.paramMap.subscribe(p => console.log(p.get('id')));            // 5
this.route.queryParamMap.subscribe(q => console.log(q.get('tab')));      // info
```

## When to use it

Path params for "which item"; query params for "how to show the list".

topics.title: What are wildcard and default routes in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A default route redirects the empty path to a start page. A wildcard route (`**`) catches any URL that matches nothing, usually to show a 404 page.

---

## Explanation

Angular checks routes from top to bottom, so the wildcard must be last. `pathMatch: 'full'` makes the redirect happen only when the whole URL is empty.

## Example

```text
export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', redirectTo: 'dashboard', pathMatch: 'full' },
  { path: 'dashboard', component: DashboardComponent },
  { path: '**', component: NotFoundComponent }
];
```

## When to use it

Every app should have both.

topics.title: How do you store static data in a route?
topics.body:
## Know it

A route has a `data` property for fixed values such as a page title, a required role, or breadcrumb text.

---

## Explanation

Read it with `route.snapshot.data` or `route.data`. Guards often use it to check the required role.

## Example

```text
{ path: 'reports', component: ReportsComponent, data: { title: 'Reports', role: 'Admin' } }

const role = inject(ActivatedRoute).snapshot.data['role'];   // 'Admin'
```

## When to use it

Use it to configure guards and page titles without writing extra code.

topics.title: How do you implement role-based access in Angular?
What is the difference between reactive forms and template-driven forms?
topics.body:
## Know it

Reactive forms are built in TypeScript with `FormGroup` and `FormControl`. Template-driven forms are built in the HTML with `ngModel`, and Angular creates the form model for you.

---

## Explanation

Reactive forms give more control, are easier to test, and suit complex or dynamic forms. Template-driven forms need less code and suit small forms.

## Example

```text
// reactive
form = new FormGroup({
  email: new FormControl('', [Validators.required, Validators.email])
});
<input formControlName="email">

// template-driven
<input name="email" [(ngModel)]="email" required email>
```

## When to use it

Reactive for real applications; template-driven for a quick simple form.

topics.title: What is a FormGroup in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `FormGroup` groups several form controls into one object, so you can read the value and validity of the whole form at once.

---

## Explanation

`form.value` is an object with every control's value. `form.valid` is true only if all controls are valid. Groups can be nested.

## Example

```text
form = new FormGroup({
  name: new FormControl('', Validators.required),
  age: new FormControl(18)
});
console.log(form.value);   // { name: '', age: 18 }
console.log(form.valid);   // false (name is empty)
```

## When to use it

Use it for any form with a fixed set of fields, like login or registration.

topics.title: What is a FormArray in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `FormArray` holds a dynamic list of controls or groups, so the user can add and remove rows.

---

## Explanation

You add with `push()` and remove with `removeAt()`. The template loops over `array.controls`.

## Example

```text
form = new FormGroup({ skills: new FormArray([new FormControl('')]) });
get skills() { return this.form.get('skills') as FormArray; }

add()          { this.skills.push(new FormControl('')); }
remove(i: number) { this.skills.removeAt(i); }
```

## When to use it

Use it for repeating fields such as skills, phone numbers, or invoice lines.

topics.title: What is the difference between FormGroup and FormArray?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `FormGroup` has named controls in a fixed shape. A `FormArray` has an ordered list of controls whose size can change.

---

## Explanation

In a group you access a control by name (`form.get('name')`). In an array you access it by index (`array.at(0)`).

## Example

```text
new FormGroup({ name: new FormControl('') })    // { name: '' }
new FormArray([new FormControl('a'), new FormControl('b')])   // ['a', 'b']
```

## When to use it

Group for a known set of fields; array when the user decides how many.

topics.title: What is FormBuilder in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`FormBuilder` is a helper service that creates groups, controls, and arrays with less code.

---

## Explanation

It does the same as `new FormGroup(...)` and `new FormControl(...)`, but with a shorter syntax.

## Example

```text
private fb = inject(FormBuilder);

form = this.fb.group({
  name: ['', Validators.required],
  email: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.email]]
});
```

## When to use it

Use it whenever you build reactive forms.

topics.title: What is a custom validator in Angular?
What is an async validator in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

An async validator checks a value by waiting for something, like an API call, and returns an Observable or Promise of the error object or `null`.

---

## Explanation

Angular runs async validators only after the sync validators pass. While waiting, the control status is `PENDING`. Add `debounceTime` so you do not call the API on every keystroke.

## Example

```text
export function uniqueEmail(api: UserService): AsyncValidatorFn {
  return (c: AbstractControl) =>
    timer(400).pipe(
      switchMap(() => api.emailExists(c.value)),
      map(exists => (exists ? { emailTaken: true } : null))
    );
}
email = new FormControl('', { asyncValidators: [uniqueEmail(this.api)] });
```

## When to use it

Use it for checks that need the server, such as "is this username free?".

topics.title: What is cross-field validation in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Cross-field validation checks two or more fields together, for example that a password and its confirmation match. It is placed on the `FormGroup`, not on a single control.

---

## Explanation

The validator receives the group, reads both controls, and returns an error on the group. In the template you read `form.errors?.['mismatch']`.

## Example

```text
const match: ValidatorFn = (g: AbstractControl) =>
  g.get('password')?.value === g.get('confirm')?.value ? null : { mismatch: true };

form = new FormGroup({
  password: new FormControl(''),
  confirm: new FormControl('')
}, { validators: match });
```

## When to use it

Use it for rules that depend on more than one field: matching passwords, date ranges, totals.

topics.title: What is ControlValueAccessor in Angular?
What is forwardRef in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`forwardRef` lets you refer to a class that is not defined yet at that line of code, so Angular resolves it later.

---

## Explanation

In a decorator, the class itself does not exist when the decorator is evaluated, so referring to it directly gives `undefined`. `forwardRef(() => MyClass)` delays the lookup.

## Example

```text
providers: [{
  provide: NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR,
  useExisting: forwardRef(() => MyInputComponent),   // the class is defined below
  multi: true
}]
export class MyInputComponent {}
```

## When to use it

You will see it mainly with `ControlValueAccessor` providers.

topics.title: What are dynamic forms in Angular?
What is a pipe in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it A pipe transforms a value for display in a template, without changing the original value. Examples: `date`, `currency`, `uppercase`, `async`. --- ## Explanation You write it with the `|` symbol. Pipes can take arguments and can be chained. You can create custom pipes with `@Pipe`. ## Example ```text

{{ today | date:'dd/MM/yyyy' }}

{{ price | currency:'INR' }}

{{ name | uppercase }}

@Pipe({ name: 'initials', standalone: true }) export class InitialsPipe implements PipeTransform { transform(v: string) { return v.split(' ').map(x => x[0]).join(''); } } ``` ## When to use it Use it for display formatting in templates.

topics.title: What is the difference between a pure pipe and an impure pipe?
topics.body:
## Know it

A pure pipe runs only when its input value or reference changes. An impure pipe runs on every change detection pass.

---

## Explanation

Pure is the default and is fast. Impure (`pure: false`) is needed only if the pipe depends on something other than its input, but it can hurt performance, so avoid it for heavy work.

## Example

```text
@Pipe({ name: 'filter' })                    // pure: not re-run when you push to the same array
@Pipe({ name: 'filterLive', pure: false })   // impure: re-run on every check
```

## When to use it

Keep pipes pure; make one impure only when you must see in-place changes.

topics.title: What is the async pipe in Angular?
What are directives in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it Directives add behavior to elements in a template. There are three kinds: components (with a template), structural directives (change the DOM structure), and attribute directives (change look or behavior). --- ## Explanation A component is really a directive with a template. Structural ones add or remove elements (`*ngIf`, `*ngFor`). Attribute ones change an existing element (`ngClass`, `ngStyle`). ## Example ```text
Structural: adds or removes this element
Attribute: changes the class
``` ## When to use it Use directives to reuse template behavior without writing a new component.

topics.title: What is the difference between structural and attribute directives?
topics.body:
## Know it Structural directives add or remove elements from the DOM (`*ngIf`, `*ngFor`). Attribute directives only change how an existing element looks or behaves (`ngClass`, `ngStyle`). --- ## Explanation Structural ones are written with a `*` and work with `` behind the scenes. Attribute ones are written like a normal attribute and never change the DOM structure. ## Example ```text
  • {{ i }}

    • Red text

    ``` ## When to use it Choose structural to show or repeat content; attribute to style or react to events.

topics.title: How do you create a custom directive in Angular?
What is exportAs in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `exportAs` gives a directive a name so a template reference variable can point to the directive instance and use its public methods. --- ## Explanation Without it, `#ref` points to the element. With `#ref="name"` it points to the directive. ## Example ```text @Directive({ selector: '[appToggle]', exportAs: 'toggle', standalone: true }) export class ToggleDirective { open = false; flip() { this.open = !this.open; } }
``` ## When to use it Use it to control a directive from the template.

topics.title: What is ng-container and ng-template?
topics.body:
## Know it `` groups elements without adding an extra element to the DOM. `` defines a template that is not shown until Angular is told to render it. --- ## Explanation `ng-container` is useful when you need a structural directive but do not want an extra `div`. `ng-template` is used for else blocks and passing templates to components, and is what `*ngIf` uses behind the scenes. ## Example ```text

Welcome

Has items

No items

 ``` ## When to use it `ng-container` to group; `ng-template` for reusable or conditional template parts.

How does Angular protect against XSS?
topics.body:
## Know it Angular treats every value as untrusted and sanitizes it before putting it in the DOM. `DomSanitizer` lets you mark a value as trusted when you are sure it is safe. --- ## Explanation When you bind HTML with `[innerHTML]`, Angular removes dangerous parts like `'; //
-> shows bold Hi, the script is removed safe = this.sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml(cmsHtml); // only for content you fully trust ``` ## When to use it Rely on the default; bypass only for trusted content, such as HTML from your own CMS.

topics.title: What are environment files in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Environment files hold values that change between development and production, such as the API URL and feature flags. The build swaps the right file in.

---

## Explanation

`angular.json` has `fileReplacements` that replace `environment.ts` with `environment.prod.ts` for production builds. Never put secrets in them, because the code ships to the browser.

## Example

```text
// environment.ts
export const environment = { production: false, apiUrl: 'http://localhost:3000/api' };

import { environment } from '../environments/environment';
this.http.get(environment.apiUrl + '/users');
```

## When to use it

Use them for anything that differs per environment, except secrets.

How do you test a component in Angular?
