What is Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it Angular is a TypeScript-based frontend framework from Google for building single page applications. --- ## Explanation It includes components, templates, dependency injection, routing, forms, and an HTTP client, so you do not need many extra libraries. ## Example ```text @Component({ selector: 'app-hello', standalone: true, template: `

Hello {{ name }}

` }) export class HelloComponent { name = 'Angular'; } ``` ## When to use it Choose it for large, long-lived apps that benefit from structure, such as dashboards and ERPs.

topics.title: What are the building blocks of Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

The main building blocks are components, templates, modules (or standalone components), services with dependency injection, and routing.

---

## Explanation

A component controls a piece of the UI. A template is its HTML. Services hold shared logic. DI delivers services. Routing moves between views.

## Example

```text
Component  -> app-user (class + template + css)
Service    -> UserService (API calls)
DI         -> inject(UserService)
Routing    -> { path: 'users', component: UserComponent }
```

## When to use it

Use this as the mental map when you explain Angular to anyone.

topics.title: What is a single page application (SPA)?
topics.body:
## Know it

A SPA loads one HTML page once and then updates the content in the browser without a full page reload.

---

## Explanation

The router swaps components in and out, and data comes from APIs. This feels faster, but it needs care for SEO, which is why SSR exists.

## Example

```text
/home  ->  router shows HomeComponent
/users ->  router shows UsersComponent     // the page never fully reloads
```

## When to use it

Good for apps behind a login; use SSR when SEO or first-load speed matters.

topics.title: What are NgModule and standalone components?
What is the difference between NgModule and standalone components?
topics.body:
## Know it

An NgModule declares and organizes many components. A standalone component declares its own dependencies and needs no module.

---

## Explanation

In modules, a component belongs to exactly one module. In standalone code, you import what you need directly into the component, and bootstrap with `bootstrapApplication`.

## Example

```text
// module
bootstrapModule(AppModule)
// standalone
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, { providers: [provideRouter(routes)] })
```

## When to use it

New projects: standalone. Existing projects: migrate step by step.

topics.title: How does Angular start and work internally?
topics.body:
## Know it

Angular starts in `main.ts`, bootstraps the root component, builds the component tree, binds data, and runs change detection to keep the view updated.

---

## Explanation

The browser loads `index.html` with `<app-root>`. `main.ts` calls `bootstrapApplication`, Angular creates the root component, its children, and then updates the DOM whenever data changes.

## Example

```text
// main.ts
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig);

// index.html
<app-root></app-root>
```

## When to use it

Useful to explain what happens between "ng serve" and the first screen.

topics.title: What is the purpose of the main Angular config files?
topics.body:
## Know it

`package.json` lists dependencies and scripts, `angular.json` configures the CLI build, `tsconfig.json` configures TypeScript, `main.ts` starts the app, and `index.html` is the page that loads.

---

## Explanation

`package-lock.json` pins exact versions so every machine installs the same packages, so it should be committed. `dependencies` are needed at runtime; `devDependencies` only during development.

## Example

```text
package.json       -> "dependencies": { "@angular/core": "^18" }, "scripts": { "start": "ng serve" }
angular.json       -> build options, assets, global styles, file replacements
tsconfig.json      -> "strict": true, "target": "ES2022"
```

## When to use it

Know them for onboarding, build problems, and deployment questions.

topics.title: What are the most used Angular CLI commands?
topics.body:
## Know it

The Angular CLI creates, runs, builds, tests, and updates an Angular project from the command line.

---

## Explanation

`ng generate` scaffolds code, `ng serve` runs a dev server, `ng build` creates a deployable build, `ng test` runs tests, `ng add` installs a library, and `ng update` upgrades Angular.

## Example

```text
ng new my-app
ng generate component user
ng serve
ng build --configuration production
ng test
ng update @angular/core @angular/cli
```

## When to use it

Use the CLI instead of creating files by hand.

topics.title: How do components communicate in Angular?
What is the difference between smart and dumb components?
What is SSR and hydration in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

SSR (server-side rendering) renders the page's HTML on the server first. Hydration then reuses that HTML in the browser and makes it interactive instead of building it again.

---

## Explanation

SSR gives a faster first view and better SEO. Without hydration, the browser would throw the server HTML away and rebuild it, causing a flicker. With it, Angular attaches event listeners to the existing DOM.

## Example

```text
ng new my-app --ssr

bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, {
  providers: [provideClientHydration()]
});
```

## When to use it

Use it for public, SEO-sensitive sites; skip it for apps behind a login.

topics.title: What are signals in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A signal is a value holder that tells Angular exactly who uses it, so only the parts of the UI that read it update when it changes.

---

## Explanation

You read a signal by calling it (`count()`), and change it with `set()` or `update()`. Angular tracks reads in templates, `computed()`, and `effect()`. No subscribe or unsubscribe is needed.

## Example

```ts
// tiny signal model so you can run it here
function signal(v) { const f = () => v; f.set = x => { v = x; }; f.update = fn => { v = fn(v); }; return f; }

const count = signal(0);
console.log(count());        // 0
count.set(5);
console.log(count());        // 5
count.update(c => c + 1);
console.log(count());        // 6
```

## When to use it

Use it for local UI state such as a toggle, selected tab, or cart count.

topics.title: Why were signals introduced in Angular?
What is computed() in Angular signals?
What is effect() in Angular signals?
What is the difference between computed() and effect()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`computed()` produces a value from other signals. `effect()` runs an action when signals change and returns nothing.

---

## Explanation

If you want a number, a string, or a list, use `computed`. If you want to log, save, or call something, use `effect`.

## Example

```text
total = computed(() => this.price() * this.qty());          // a value
effect(() => console.log('Total is', this.total()));        // an action
```

## When to use it

Default to `computed`; reach for `effect` only for real side effects.

topics.title: What are signal inputs in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Signal inputs use `input()` instead of `@Input()`, so an input is a signal you read by calling it.

---

## Explanation

They can be required (`input.required<T>()`), and you can use `computed()` and `effect()` on them directly without `ngOnChanges`.

## Example

```text
name = input.required<string>();
greeting = computed(() => 'Hello ' + this.name());

<app-hello [name]="'Ram'"></app-hello>      // greeting() -> "Hello Ram"
```

## When to use it

Use it in new components, especially with OnPush.

topics.title: What is model() in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`model()` is a writable signal for two-way binding between parent and child. It replaces an `@Input` plus an `@Output` pair.

---

## Explanation

The child can read and set the value, and the parent can bind it with `[(prop)]`. Angular creates the matching change event for you.

## Example

```text
// child
value = model(0);
inc() { this.value.update(v => v + 1); }

// parent
<app-counter [(value)]="count"></app-counter>
```

## When to use it

Use it for reusable controls such as toggles, ratings, and search boxes.

topics.title: What is toSignal() in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it `toSignal()` converts an Observable into a signal that always holds its latest value. --- ## Explanation It subscribes for you and unsubscribes when the component is destroyed. Give an `initialValue`, or the signal starts as `undefined`. ## Example ```text users = toSignal(this.api.getUsers(), { initialValue: [] }); @for (u of users(); track u.id) {

{{ u.name }}

} ``` ## When to use it Use it to read HTTP or other Observable data in a signal-based template.

topics.title: What is toObservable() in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`toObservable()` converts a signal into an Observable, so you can use RxJS operators such as `debounceTime` and `switchMap`.

---

## Explanation

It emits when the signal changes (checked in a microtask, so rapid changes may be merged into one).

## Example

```text
search = signal('');

results$ = toObservable(this.search).pipe(
  debounceTime(300),
  distinctUntilChanged(),
  switchMap(text => this.api.search(text))
);
```

## When to use it

Use it when state lives in a signal but you need RxJS timing or async operators.

topics.title: What is the difference between toSignal() and toObservable()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`toSignal()` goes from Observable to signal. `toObservable()` goes from signal to Observable.

---

## Explanation

They are the two bridges between RxJS and signals, so you can mix both styles in one app.

## Example

```text
users = toSignal(this.http.get<User[]>('/api/users'), { initialValue: [] });   // Observable -> signal
query$ = toObservable(this.queryText);                                          // signal -> Observable
```

## When to use it

Use `toSignal` for display, `toObservable` for async pipelines.

topics.title: What is linkedSignal() in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`linkedSignal()` is a writable signal whose value resets from another signal when that source changes, but the user can still set it manually.

---

## Explanation

A normal `computed` cannot be written to. A `linkedSignal` gives you a default that follows the source, plus the freedom to override it.

## Example

```text
warehouses = signal(['Nagpur', 'Pune']);
selected = linkedSignal(() => this.warehouses()[0]);   // 'Nagpur'

selected.set('Pune');          // user picks Pune
this.warehouses.set(['Delhi', 'Agra']);   // new list -> selected resets to 'Delhi'
```

## When to use it

Use it for a selection that should reset when the list changes.

topics.title: What are resource() and httpResource in Angular?
Are signals a replacement for RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

No. Signals manage state that changes over time and is read in the UI. RxJS handles async streams and events, such as HTTP, debouncing, and websockets.

---

## Explanation

Signals have a current value and no time dimension. Observables describe a sequence of values over time with operators like `switchMap`. Real apps use both, joined with `toSignal` and `toObservable`.

## Example

```text
isOpen = signal(false);                       // UI state -> signal
users$ = this.http.get('/api/users');         // async request -> RxJS
results = toSignal(users$, { initialValue: [] });   // join them
```

## When to use it

Signals for state, RxJS for async work.

topics.title: What is the difference between Observable and Promise?
What is the difference between hot and cold observables?
topics.body:
## Know it

A cold observable starts a new run for each subscriber (HTTP calls). A hot observable is already running and shares values among subscribers (DOM events, Subjects).

---

## Explanation

A late subscriber to a cold observable still gets all values from the start. A late subscriber to a hot one only gets values from the moment it joins.

## Example

```rxjs
const cold$ = rxjs.of(1, 2, 3);
cold$.subscribe(v => console.log('A', v));
cold$.subscribe(v => console.log('B', v));      // B also gets 1,2,3

const hot = new rxjs.Subject();
hot.subscribe(v => console.log('X', v));
hot.next(1);
hot.subscribe(v => console.log('Y', v));        // Y misses the 1
hot.next(2);                                     // X 2, Y 2
```

## When to use it

Know it to explain why an API is called twice, and how `shareReplay` fixes it.

topics.title: What is the difference between unicast and multicast?
topics.body:
## Know it

Unicast gives every subscriber its own execution. Multicast shares one execution among all subscribers.

---

## Explanation

Plain observables such as `HttpClient` calls are unicast, so two subscribers send two requests. A `Subject`, or `shareReplay`, makes it multicast.

## Example

```rxjs
let runs = 0;
const source$ = new rxjs.Observable(s => { runs++; s.next(runs); s.complete(); });

source$.subscribe(v => console.log('unicast', v));
source$.subscribe(v => console.log('unicast', v));    // 1 then 2 : ran twice

const shared$ = source$.pipe(rxjs.operators.shareReplay(1));
shared$.subscribe(v => console.log('multicast', v));
shared$.subscribe(v => console.log('multicast', v));  // same value: ran once
```

## When to use it

Use multicast to avoid duplicate API calls.

topics.title: What is the difference between ReplaySubject and AsyncSubject?
topics.body:
## Know it

A `ReplaySubject` replays the last N values to new subscribers. An `AsyncSubject` emits only the last value, and only when it completes.

---

## Explanation

Replay is for history, such as recent chat messages. Async is for "only the final result matters".

## Example

```rxjs
const r = new rxjs.ReplaySubject(2);
r.next(1); r.next(2); r.next(3);
r.subscribe(v => console.log('Replay', v));       // Replay 2, Replay 3

const a = new rxjs.AsyncSubject();
a.next(1); a.next(2); a.next(3);
a.subscribe(v => console.log('Async', v));
a.complete();                                      // Async 3
```

## When to use it

Replay for recent history; Async for a single final value.

topics.title: What is the difference between combineLatest, forkJoin, zip, and withLatestFrom?
What is the difference between takeUntil and takeUntilDestroyed?
What is component-based architecture in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Component-based architecture means the app is split into small, reusable, independent components. Each one has its own template, logic, and styles.

---

## Explanation

Components form a tree: a root component contains pages, pages contain smaller components. Because each piece is independent, it can be reused, tested, and changed without breaking the rest.

## Example

```text
AppComponent
 ├─ HeaderComponent
 ├─ UserListComponent
 │    └─ UserCardComponent  (reused for every user)
 └─ FooterComponent
```

## When to use it

Always: it is how every Angular app is built. Mention reusability and maintainability in interviews.

topics.title: What is Angular architecture?
topics.body:
## Know it

Angular architecture describes how an app is organized: components for the UI, services for logic and API calls, dependency injection to connect them, routing for navigation, and data binding to link class and template.

---

## Explanation

A component asks for a service through DI. The service talks to the backend through `HttpClient`. The router decides which component is on screen. Modules (or standalone components) group related features.

## Example

```text
Router -> shows UsersComponent
UsersComponent --(DI)--> UserService --(HttpClient)--> API
UsersComponent template <--(data binding)-- component class
```

## When to use it

Use this picture whenever an interviewer asks "explain Angular architecture".

topics.title: What is the purpose of index.html in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`index.html` is the one HTML page the browser loads. It contains the root tag, such as `<app-root>`, where Angular puts the app.

---

## Explanation

It also holds the page title, favicon, meta tags, and external fonts or scripts. The Angular build injects the compiled script files into it automatically.

## Example

```text
<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head><title>My App</title></head>
  <body>
    <app-root></app-root>     <!-- Angular renders the app here -->
  </body>
</html>
```

## When to use it

Edit it for the page title, SEO meta tags, and global fonts.

topics.title: What is package.json in an Angular project?
topics.body:
## Know it

`package.json` is the project's main config file. It lists the project name, dependencies, devDependencies, and npm scripts.

---

## Explanation

`npm install` reads it and installs every listed package. The `scripts` section defines commands like `npm start` and `npm run build`.

## Example

```text
{
  "name": "my-app",
  "scripts": { "start": "ng serve", "build": "ng build" },
  "dependencies": { "@angular/core": "^18.0.0", "rxjs": "~7.8.0" },
  "devDependencies": { "typescript": "~5.4.0", "@angular/cli": "^18.0.0" }
}
```

## When to use it

Edit it to add packages or scripts; usually through `npm install` rather than by hand.

topics.title: What is package-lock.json and should it be committed?
topics.body:
## Know it

`package-lock.json` is generated by npm. It records the exact version of every installed package and its sub-dependencies. Yes, you should commit it to Git.

---

## Explanation

`package.json` allows ranges like `^18.0.0`, so two machines could install different versions. The lock file pins the exact ones, so everyone gets identical builds.

## Example

```text
package.json       "rxjs": "~7.8.0"         (a range)
package-lock.json  "rxjs": "7.8.1"          (the exact version everyone installs)

npm ci      // installs exactly what the lock file says (best for CI and deployment)
```

## When to use it

Always commit it, and use `npm ci` in build pipelines.

topics.title: What is angular.json?
topics.body:
## Know it

`angular.json` is the Angular CLI's configuration file. It controls how the app is built, served, and tested.

---

## Explanation

It holds build options, global styles and scripts, assets, environment file replacements, and separate configurations such as development and production.

## Example

```text
"build": {
  "options": { "styles": ["src/styles.css"], "assets": ["src/assets"] },
  "configurations": {
    "production": { "fileReplacements": [{ "replace": "src/environments/environment.ts",
                                           "with": "src/environments/environment.prod.ts" }] }
  }
}
```

## When to use it

Edit it to add global styles such as Bootstrap, copy assets, or tune build budgets.

topics.title: What is tsconfig.json?
What is main.ts in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`main.ts` is the entry point. It is the first file that runs and it starts (bootstraps) the app.

---

## Explanation

Modern Angular calls `bootstrapApplication` with the root component and the app providers (routes, HTTP client). Older apps called `platformBrowserDynamic().bootstrapModule(AppModule)`.

## Example

```text
import { bootstrapApplication } from '@angular/platform-browser';
import { AppComponent } from './app/app.component';
import { appConfig } from './app/app.config';

bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig).catch(err => console.error(err));
```

## When to use it

Rarely edited; this is where global providers are registered.

topics.title: What is app.module.ts?
topics.body:
## Know it

`app.module.ts` is the root module of a traditional (module-based) Angular app. It groups the components, imports, and providers the app needs.

---

## Explanation

Its `@NgModule` has `declarations` (components, directives, pipes), `imports` (other modules), `providers` (services), and `bootstrap` (the first component). New apps use standalone components and `app.config.ts` instead.

## Example

```text
@NgModule({
  declarations: [AppComponent, UserListComponent],
  imports: [BrowserModule, HttpClientModule, RouterModule.forRoot(routes)],
  providers: [],
  bootstrap: [AppComponent]
})
export class AppModule {}
```

## When to use it

You will meet it in older codebases; know it for maintenance and migration questions.

topics.title: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
topics.body:
## Know it

`dependencies` are packages the app needs to run. `devDependencies` are packages needed only while developing, building, and testing.

---

## Explanation

Users of the finished app never need the dev packages. In an Angular app, `@angular/core` and `rxjs` are dependencies; the CLI, TypeScript, ESLint, and test tools are devDependencies.

## Example

```text
npm install rxjs            // goes to dependencies
npm install -D typescript   // goes to devDependencies
```

## When to use it

Use it to decide where each package belongs, and to explain build vs runtime needs.

topics.title: What is a component in Angular, and what does it contain?
topics.body:
## Know it

A component controls one part of the screen. It is made of a TypeScript class (logic), an HTML template (view), and CSS (styles), tied together by the `@Component` decorator.

---

## Explanation

The decorator's `selector` is the HTML tag you use to place it. Every Angular app has at least one component, the root component.

## Example

```text
@Component({
  selector: 'app-greeting',
  standalone: true,
  templateUrl: './greeting.component.html',
  styleUrl: './greeting.component.css'
})
export class GreetingComponent { name = 'Ram'; }

// <app-greeting></app-greeting>
```

## When to use it

Create a component for every reusable or self-contained piece of UI.

topics.title: What is a selector in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it A selector is the custom HTML tag (or attribute) that places a component or directive in a template. --- ## Explanation Components usually use an element selector like `app-card`. Directives usually use an attribute selector like `[appHighlight]`. A prefix such as `app-` avoids clashes with real HTML tags. ## Example ```text @Component({ selector: 'app-card', template: '...' }) // @Directive({ selector: '[appHighlight]' }) //

``` ## When to use it Choose a clear, prefixed name for every component and directive.

topics.title: What is the difference between template and templateUrl?
topics.body:
## Know it `template` holds the HTML inside the decorator. `templateUrl` points to a separate HTML file. --- ## Explanation Inline templates suit very small components. Separate files are easier to read and maintain, so real projects mostly use `templateUrl`. ## Example ```text @Component({ selector: 'app-hi', template: `

Hello

` }) // inline @Component({ selector: 'app-hi', templateUrl: './hi.component.html' }) // separate file ``` ## When to use it Inline for tiny components; separate files for everything else.

topics.title: How does dynamic component loading work in Angular?
What is Ivy in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Ivy is Angular's modern compiler and rendering engine. It produces smaller, faster code and gives better error messages.

---

## Explanation

It compiles each component on its own, which allows better tree shaking, faster builds, and features such as lazy-loading single components. It has been the default since Angular 9 and the only engine since Angular 12.

## Example

```text
// You write the same code. Ivy changes what it compiles to:
// smaller bundles, faster rebuilds, clearer template errors.
```

## When to use it

Mention it when asked why modern Angular bundles are smaller than older ones.

topics.title: How do you share data between unrelated components?
What are the ways to pass data between components in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

The options are: `@Input` (parent to child), `@Output` with `EventEmitter` (child to parent), a shared service with Subject or BehaviorSubject, router parameters, global state (NgRx), and signals.

---

## Explanation

Pick by relationship. Near each other: input and output. Far apart: service. Between pages: route params or query params. Big apps: a store.

## Example

```text
<app-child [data]="info" (changed)="onChange($event)"></app-child>   // @Input + @Output
this.router.navigate(['/user', 5]);                                    // route param
cart.add();                                                            // shared service
```

## When to use it

Use the simplest option that fits; do not reach for a store for parent and child.

topics.title: What is state management in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

State management is how an app stores, updates, and shares data such as the logged-in user, API results, form data, and UI flags like "loading".

---

## Explanation

Small apps are fine with a service holding a `BehaviorSubject` or signals. Large apps use a library like NgRx, NGXS, or Akita to keep updates predictable.

## Example

```text
// small: a signal in a service
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class UiState { sidebarOpen = signal(false); toggle() { this.sidebarOpen.update(v => !v); } }
```

## When to use it

Start with a service; move to a store only when many parts of the app change the same data.

topics.title: What is NgRx?
What is the difference between smart and dumb components, and why use the split?
What is ngAfterContentChecked in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`ngAfterContentChecked` runs after every check of the projected content (`ng-content`), including the first one.

---

## Explanation

It runs very often, so keep it light. It is mainly for debugging or reacting to changes in projected content. `ngAfterViewChecked` is the same idea for the component's own view.

## Example

```text
ngAfterContentChecked() {
  console.log('projected content was checked');   // runs on every change detection pass
}
```

## When to use it

Rarely; prefer `ngAfterContentInit` unless you need a check on every pass.

topics.title: Why is OnPush faster than Default?
topics.body:
## Know it

OnPush skips a component, and everything below it, unless one of its triggers happens. Default checks every component on every pass.

---

## Explanation

Triggers are: an input reference change, an event inside the component, an `async` pipe emission, a changed signal, or `markForCheck`. Immutable data makes the reference comparison cheap, so most of the tree is skipped.

## Example

```text
// 1,000 rows, one changed
Default: checks all 1,000 components
OnPush:  checks only the row whose input reference changed
```

## When to use it

Use it to answer "how do you make a big Angular app fast".

topics.title: Why use pipe() before subscribe()?
topics.body:
## Know it

`pipe()` lets you transform, filter, and control a stream with operators before the result reaches `subscribe()`.

---

## Explanation

Without it, all the logic lives inside `subscribe`. With it, the stream does the work (map, filter, debounce, handle errors) and `subscribe` just uses the final value.

## Example

```rxjs
const { of } = rxjs;
const { map, filter } = rxjs.operators;

of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).pipe(
  filter(n => n % 2 === 1),
  map(n => n * 10)
).subscribe(v => console.log(v));
// 10, 30, 50
```

## When to use it

Always apply operators with `pipe()`; keep `subscribe()` for the final action.

topics.title: What is @Injectable in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

`@Injectable()` marks a class so Angular can create it and inject its own dependencies. With `providedIn: 'root'` it also registers the service app-wide.

---

## Explanation

Angular needs the decorator to read the constructor's types. With `providedIn: 'root'` the service is a singleton and is removed from the bundle if nothing uses it (tree-shakable).

## Example

```text
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class UserService {
  constructor(private http: HttpClient) {}
}
```

## When to use it

Put it on every service.

topics.title: Can an Angular service work without @Injectable?
topics.body:
## Know it

Yes, but only if the service has no constructor dependencies and you provide it manually. If it needs anything injected, `@Injectable()` is required.

---

## Explanation

Without the decorator, TypeScript does not emit the constructor parameter types, so Angular cannot tell what to inject. A class with an empty constructor needs no types.

## Example

```text
export class Logger { log(m: string) { console.log(m); } }       // OK: no dependencies
export class Api { constructor(private http: HttpClient) {} }    // needs @Injectable()
```

## When to use it

Add `@Injectable()` anyway, so nothing breaks when you add a dependency later.

topics.title: What are providers in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A provider tells Angular how to create a dependency. The common forms are `useClass`, `useValue`, `useFactory`, and `useExisting`.

---

## Explanation

Providers can be set at root level (`providedIn: 'root'`, or `app.config.ts`), per route, or per component. The place decides who shares the instance.

## Example

```text
providers: [
  UserService,                                          // shorthand for useClass: UserService
  { provide: API_URL, useValue: 'https://api.test' },
  { provide: Logger, useClass: ConsoleLogger },
  { provide: Config, useFactory: () => new Config(inject(API_URL)) }
]
```

## When to use it

Use them to configure services, swap implementations, and supply config values.

topics.title: What is a singleton service in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

A singleton service has exactly one instance shared by the whole app. `providedIn: 'root'` creates one.

---

## Explanation

Every component that injects it gets the same object, so data stored in it is shared. A service listed in a component's `providers` is not a singleton; each component instance gets its own.

## Example

```text
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class CounterService { value = 0; }

// two components inject CounterService -> they see the same value
```

## When to use it

Use it for shared state and shared logic such as auth and caching.

topics.title: How do you call an API in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Provide `HttpClient`, inject it into a service, call `get`, `post`, `put`, or `delete`, and subscribe in the component or use the `async` pipe.

---

## Explanation

Each method returns a cold Observable, so nothing is sent until someone subscribes. Keep API calls in services, not in components.

## Example

```text
// app.config.ts
provideHttpClient()

// service
getUsers() { return this.http.get<User[]>('/api/users'); }

// component
users$ = this.userService.getUsers();     // <li *ngFor="let u of users$ | async">
```

## When to use it

This is the standard pattern for every backend call.

topics.title: What is SSR in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

SSR (server-side rendering) means the server builds the page's HTML first and sends it to the browser, instead of the browser building it.

---

## Explanation

The user sees content sooner, and search engines can read it. Angular does this with `@angular/ssr` (previously Angular Universal). Code that uses `window` or `document` must be guarded because it also runs on the server.

## Example

```text
ng add @angular/ssr
// Without SSR: browser downloads JS -> builds page -> shows it
// With SSR:    server sends ready HTML -> shows immediately -> Angular takes over
```

## When to use it

Use it for public, SEO-sensitive pages; skip it for private dashboards.

topics.title: What is hydration in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Hydration makes a server-rendered page interactive by attaching Angular to the existing HTML instead of rebuilding it.

---

## Explanation

Without hydration the page is visible but buttons and forms do nothing, or the page flickers when the client re-renders. With it, Angular reuses the DOM and just adds events and state.

## Example

```text
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, {
  providers: [provideClientHydration()]
});
```

## When to use it

Enable it whenever you use SSR.

topics.title: What is RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

RxJS is a library for handling asynchronous data as streams. It is built around Observables and operators that transform them.

---

## Explanation

Angular uses it for HTTP calls, form value changes, router events, and more. You create or receive an Observable, shape it with operators in `pipe()`, and react in `subscribe()`.

## Example

```rxjs
const { interval } = rxjs;
const { take, map } = rxjs.operators;

interval(100).pipe(take(3), map(n => n * 2)).subscribe(v => console.log(v));
// 0, 2, 4
```

## When to use it

Use it for anything that arrives over time: API calls, typing, clicks, sockets.

topics.title: What is an Observer in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

An Observer is the object, or set of functions, that receives values from an Observable: `next` for values, `error` for failure, and `complete` for the end.

---

## Explanation

The object you pass to `subscribe()` is the Observer. The Observable calls its methods as events happen.

## Example

```rxjs
const obs$ = new rxjs.Observable(s => { s.next('a'); s.next('b'); s.complete(); });

obs$.subscribe({
  next: v => console.log('value', v),
  error: e => console.log('error', e),
  complete: () => console.log('done')
});
// value a, value b, done
```

## When to use it

Pass all three callbacks when you must react to errors and completion too.

topics.title: What is the difference between an Observable and an Observer?
topics.body:
## Know it

An Observable is the source that produces values. An Observer is the listener that receives them. `subscribe()` connects the two.

---

## Explanation

The Observable describes what to send and when. The Observer describes what to do with each value, error, and completion.

## Example

```rxjs
const source$ = rxjs.of(1, 2);                       // Observable: produces
source$.subscribe({ next: v => console.log(v) });    // Observer: consumes
```

## When to use it

Use it as a one-line answer: "Observable sends, Observer receives".

topics.title: Why does Angular use Observables instead of Promises?
topics.body:
## Know it

Observables can emit many values, can be cancelled, are lazy, and come with powerful operators. Promises give one value, cannot be cancelled, and start immediately.

---

## Explanation

This matters for search boxes (cancel old requests), live events (many values), and retries. Operators like `switchMap` and `debounceTime` have no Promise equivalent.

## Example

```rxjs
const { timer } = rxjs;
const sub = timer(1000).subscribe(() => console.log('never printed'));
sub.unsubscribe();            // cancelled - a Promise could not be cancelled
console.log('cancelled before it fired');
```

## When to use it

Mention cancellation and multiple values first; they are the strongest points.

topics.title: How do you handle asynchronous operations in Angular?
topics.body:
## Know it

Mostly with RxJS Observables (`HttpClient`, `valueChanges`), subscribed manually or through the `async` pipe. Simple cases can use Promises with `async` and `await`, or signals with `resource`.

---

## Explanation

Observables are preferred because they can be cancelled and combined. The `async` pipe handles subscribing and unsubscribing for you.

## Example

```text
users$ = this.http.get<User[]>('/api/users');       // Observable + async pipe

async load() {                                        // Promise style
  const users = await firstValueFrom(this.http.get<User[]>('/api/users'));
}
```

## When to use it

Observables for streams and cancellation; `await` for one-off calls.

topics.title: What is an AsyncSubject in RxJS?
What does throttleTime() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`throttleTime(ms)` lets the first value through immediately, then ignores all values for the next `ms` milliseconds.

---

## Explanation

It limits how often something can fire. After the window ends, the next value can pass.

## Example

```rxjs
const { interval } = rxjs;
const { throttleTime, take } = rxjs.operators;

interval(100).pipe(take(10), throttleTime(350)).subscribe(v => console.log(v));
// 0, 4, 8   (one value per 350ms window)
```

## When to use it

Use it for scroll, resize, and double-click prevention.

topics.title: What is the difference between debounceTime and throttleTime?
What does zip() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`zip` pairs the values of several Observables by position: the first with the first, the second with the second, and so on.

---

## Explanation

It waits until every source has produced its next value, then emits them together as an array. It completes when the shortest source completes.

## Example

```rxjs
const { of, zip } = rxjs;
zip(of('Q1', 'Q2', 'Q3'), of('A1', 'A2')).subscribe(v => console.log(v));
// ['Q1','A1'], ['Q2','A2']   (Q3 has no partner)
```

## When to use it

Use it when values must stay matched one to one, such as questions and answers.

topics.title: What does withLatestFrom() do in RxJS?
What does race() do in RxJS?
topics.body:
## Know it

`race` subscribes to several Observables and uses only the one that emits first. The others are cancelled.

---

## Explanation

The winner is decided by the first emission of any kind. Useful for fallbacks and timeouts.

## Example

```rxjs
const { timer, race } = rxjs;
const { map } = rxjs.operators;

race(
  timer(300).pipe(map(() => 'slow API')),
  timer(100).pipe(map(() => 'fast API'))
).subscribe(v => console.log(v));
// fast API
```

## When to use it

Use it to take the fastest of several sources, or to combine a request with a timeout.

topics.title: What does takeUntilDestroyed() do?
topics.body:
## Know it

`takeUntilDestroyed()` completes a stream automatically when the component (or the injection context) is destroyed. It was added in Angular 16.

---

## Explanation

Inside a constructor or field initializer you can call it with no argument. In other places, pass a `DestroyRef`. It replaces the manual `destroy$` Subject.

## Example

```text
private destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef);

ngOnInit() {
  interval(1000)
    .pipe(takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef))
    .subscribe(n => console.log(n));          // stops when the component is destroyed
}
```

## When to use it

Use it for every long-living subscription in new Angular code.

topics.title: Scenario: A Signal value changes, but the UI does not show the expected update. What would you check?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would verify that the template reads the signal by calling it, that the code updates the signal through its setter or `update()`, and that the UI is not displaying a stale copied value. I would also inspect any derived `computed()` signals and conditions.

---

## Explanation

Signals should be read as `count()` in the template and updated with `count.set(...)` or `count.update(...)`.

## Example

```ts
count.update(value => value + 1);
```

## When to use it

Use when debugging signal-driven state.

topics.title: Scenario: An object input changes internally, but an OnPush child does not update as expected. Why?
topics.body:
## Know it

If the parent mutates an object in place, the reference stays the same, so the child may not receive a changed input reference. I would prefer an immutable update that creates a new object reference and confirm the child template is bound to the current input.

---

## Explanation

OnPush has multiple triggers, but mutating an input in place is a common source of stale UI.

## Example

```ts
this.user = { ...this.user, active: true };
```

## When to use it

Use when data is passed through component inputs.

topics.title: Scenario: A search box sends an API request after every keystroke. How would you improve it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use the reactive form control's `valueChanges` with `debounceTime()`, `distinctUntilChanged()`, and `switchMap()`. This reduces requests, skips repeated terms, and switches to the latest search.

---

## Explanation

I would also trim or normalize the input if that matches the search requirements.

## Example

```ts
this.searchControl.valueChanges.pipe(
  map(value => value.trim()),
  debounceTime(300),
  distinctUntilChanged(),
  switchMap(term => this.api.search(term))
);
```

## When to use it

Use for autocomplete and live search.

topics.title: Scenario: An Angular component subscribes to a long-lived stream. How would you avoid a memory leak?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would prefer the `async` pipe for template-only subscriptions. For imperative subscriptions, I would use the project's supported cleanup pattern, such as `takeUntilDestroyed()` in a suitable injection context, or an explicit destroy notifier when appropriate.

---

## Explanation

Finite HttpClient calls usually complete, but streams such as subjects and DOM events may remain active.

topics.title: Scenario: Two components need to share the same user data. Where would you put the shared state?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would consider a shared service that owns the state and exposes a clear API, using signals or RxJS depending on the application's existing patterns. Both components would consume that shared source rather than maintaining unrelated copies.

topics.title: Scenario: A route should be accessible only after a user is authenticated. What would you use?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use a route guard to control navigation based on authentication state and redirect when necessary. The backend must still enforce authorization because a frontend guard can be bypassed.

topics.title: Scenario: Every API request needs an authentication header. Where should that logic go?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use an HTTP interceptor so the header logic is centralized rather than repeated in each service. I would ensure the token is added only to the appropriate requests and avoid exposing credentials to unintended origins.

topics.title: Scenario: Three independent HTTP requests must finish before rendering a summary. How would you combine them?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use `forkJoin()` for finite HTTP Observables and handle errors according to whether all results are mandatory. It emits the combined result after all sources complete.

topics.title: Scenario: One API call fails, but the page should still show results from the other API calls. What would you do?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would decide whether each result can fail independently. If so, I would catch errors inside each request and return a suitable fallback before combining them, so one failure does not automatically fail the whole combination.

topics.title: Scenario: A loading spinner stays visible after an HTTP error. How would you fix it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would reset the loading state in `finalize()` so it runs on completion, error, or unsubscription. I would also ensure errors are handled so the user sees an appropriate message.

topics.title: Scenario: A form has many dynamic controls and cross-field validation. Which form approach would you choose?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would choose reactive forms because the form model is defined in TypeScript and supports dynamic controls, validators, and group-level validation in a structured way.

topics.title: Scenario: A reusable component must render different content supplied by its parent. What Angular feature would you use?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would use content projection with `ng-content` when the parent supplies markup for the component to render. For deferred or conditional template rendering, I would consider `ng-template` and the relevant outlet or view APIs.

topics.title: Scenario: A large table makes the Angular page slow. What would you investigate first?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would measure the bottleneck first, then check the number of rendered rows, expensive template expressions, repeated computations, unstable list tracking, and unnecessary change detection. Depending on the results, I would consider pagination or virtual scrolling, stable tracking, memoized/derived values, and moving genuinely CPU-heavy work off the main thread.

topics.title: Scenario: An API response should be cached for multiple subscribers. What RxJS option might help?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would consider `shareReplay()` when sharing a finite HTTP result among subscribers. I would decide how errors, refetching, and cache lifetime should work instead of assuming it is a permanent cache.

topics.title: Scenario: A service should have separate state for each instance of a component. How would you configure it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would provide the service at the component level. Angular then creates an instance in that component's injector scope, which is useful when each component instance needs isolated state.

topics.title: Scenario: A user navigates away while a long-running request or stream is active. What should happen?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would make sure component-owned subscriptions are cleaned up when the component is destroyed. I would choose the cleanup strategy based on whether the stream is template-bound, finite, or long-lived, and whether cancellation is appropriate.

topics.title: Scenario: A reusable service needs an environment-specific configuration value. How can Angular provide it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would define an `InjectionToken` and register the configuration with `useValue` or `useFactory`, depending on whether it is already available or must be loaded or derived. I would keep configuration loading and error behavior explicit.

topics.title: Scenario: A child component must notify the parent after saving a record. How would you design it?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would expose an output event from the child and emit a clear payload after the save succeeds. The parent can then refresh its state or list without tightly coupling the child to the parent.

topics.title: Scenario: A component repeatedly calls an expensive method from its template. What would you change?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would avoid expensive work in template expressions because they may run during change detection. I would precompute or derive the value, use a pure pipe when suitable, or use a computed signal for signal-based state, after measuring the actual bottleneck.

topics.title: Scenario: An Angular route loads a rarely used feature. How can you reduce the initial bundle?
topics.body:
## Know it

I would lazy-load the feature route or component so its code is loaded when the user navigates there. I would verify the generated bundles and network behavior to confirm the benefit.

topics.title: Source Maps
topics.body:
**One-line summary of the topic.**

## Key points
- In Angular, a source map is a JSON file that maps your compiled, minified JavaScript bundle back to your original TypeScript source code. This allows you to debug your TypeScript code directly inside the browser's developer tools, even though the browser is actually executing optimized JavaScript.`code`

topics.title: Scenario: Several API calls fail with 401 at the same moment because the token expired. How would you refresh the token only once?
Scenario: You see "ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError" in the console. What causes it and how do you fix it?
Scenario: A form with 80 controls feels slow while typing. What would you do?
Scenario: A failed API call should be retried a few times before showing an error. How would you do it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use the `retry` operator with a count and a delay, and only retry errors that can succeed later, such as network errors or 503. Do not retry 400 or 401.

---

## Explanation

`retry({ count, delay })` can wait longer each time (exponential backoff). After the last attempt, `catchError` shows the message. Retrying a non-idempotent POST can create duplicates, so be careful there.

## Example

```text
this.http.get<Data>('/api/report').pipe(
  retry({
    count: 3,
    delay: (err, attempt) => (err.status >= 500 || err.status === 0) ? timer(attempt * 1000) : throwError(() => err)
  }),
  catchError(() => { this.toast.show('Server is not responding'); return EMPTY; })
);
```

## When to use it

Use it for safe GET requests on unreliable networks.

topics.title: Scenario: Users switch quickly between tabs and an older tab's data appears. How would you fix it?
topics.body:
## Know it

This is a race condition. I would drive the request from the selected tab stream with `switchMap`, so each new tab cancels the previous request.

---

## Explanation

Without cancelling, a slow old response can arrive after a newer one and overwrite it. `switchMap` unsubscribes from the older request, so only the latest result is used.

## Example

```text
selectedTab$ = new BehaviorSubject<string>('summary');

data$ = this.selectedTab$.pipe(
  distinctUntilChanged(),
  switchMap(tab => this.api.getTabData(tab))
);
// template: data$ | async
```

## When to use it

Use it wherever the latest user choice must win: tabs, filters, search.

topics.title: Scenario: The app's memory keeps growing as users navigate between pages. How would you find the cause?
Scenario: An existing module-based app must move to standalone components. How would you approach it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Migrate step by step with the Angular schematic, not all at once. Convert leaf components first, keep the app working after each step, and switch the bootstrap and routing last.

---

## Explanation

The CLI has a three-step migration: convert declarations to standalone, remove unnecessary NgModules, then switch to `bootstrapApplication`. Standalone components can still import old modules, so both styles can live together while you migrate. Run the tests after each step.

## Example

```text
ng generate @angular/core:standalone      // choose each step in turn
// 1. convert components, directives and pipes to standalone
// 2. remove unused NgModules
// 3. bootstrap with bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig)
```

## When to use it

Use it for modernization questions on older codebases.

topics.title: Scenario: A menu item and a button must be visible only to certain roles. How would you implement it?
Scenario: Live data (prices, notifications) must update in the page in real time. What would you use?
Scenario: A list with 10,000 rows must scroll smoothly. What would you do?
topics.body:
## Know it I would use virtual scrolling (Angular CDK) so only the visible rows exist in the DOM, or server-side paging, together with `track` and OnPush. --- ## Explanation Rendering 10,000 DOM nodes is slow no matter how well you code. Virtual scroll renders only what is on screen. If the data itself is huge, page it on the server and load more on demand. ## Example ```text
{{ row.name }}
 ``` ## When to use it Use it for long lists, logs, and big tables.

topics.title: Scenario: Users upload large files and need to see a progress bar. How would you build it?
Scenario: The same master-data API is called by five components. How would you avoid repeated calls?
Scenario: You want one place that handles every uncaught error in the app. What would you use?
Scenario: The API URL must be changed after deployment without rebuilding the app. How would you do it?
Scenario: A route needs data from its parent route and its own route. How do you read both?
topics.body:
## Know it

Read the parent's data through `ActivatedRoute.parent`, or set `paramsInheritanceStrategy: 'always'` so child routes inherit params and data from the parent.

---

## Explanation

By default a child route sees only its own params unless the parent is a component-less route. You can configure inheritance or walk up with `route.parent`.

## Example

```text
provideRouter(routes, withRouterConfig({ paramsInheritanceStrategy: 'always' }))

// child component
const orderId = this.route.parent?.snapshot.paramMap.get('orderId');
```

## When to use it

Use it for nested routes such as `/orders/:orderId/items/:itemId`.

topics.title: Scenario: A dashboard shows different widgets depending on the user's role. How would you build it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Keep a list of widget configs for the role, and create each widget component dynamically with `ViewContainerRef.createComponent` (or `NgComponentOutlet`).

---

## Explanation

The template does not hardcode every widget. A config maps a widget name to a component class. This keeps the dashboard open to new widgets without editing the template.

## Example

```text
widgets = [{ type: 'sales', comp: SalesWidgetComponent }, { type: 'tasks', comp: TasksWidgetComponent }];

@for (w of widgets; track w.type) {
  <ng-container *ngComponentOutlet="w.comp"></ng-container>
}
```

## When to use it

Use it for configurable dashboards and role-based screens.

topics.title: Scenario: A user logs out in one browser tab and the other tabs should log out too. How would you do it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Listen to the browser `storage` event (or use `BroadcastChannel`). When one tab clears the token, the other tabs receive the event and navigate to login.

---

## Explanation

The `storage` event fires in other tabs, not the tab that made the change. Wrap it in an Observable inside the auth service and call logout when the token key is removed.

## Example

```text
constructor() {
  fromEvent<StorageEvent>(window, 'storage').pipe(
    filter(e => e.key === 'token' && e.newValue === null),
    takeUntilDestroyed()
  ).subscribe(() => this.router.navigate(['/login']));
}
```

## When to use it

Use it for security-sensitive apps that support multiple tabs.

topics.title: Scenario: A form should save a draft automatically while the user types. How would you design it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Listen to `form.valueChanges`, debounce it, ignore unchanged values, and save with `switchMap` so a new change cancels the older save.

---

## Explanation

Saving on every keystroke wastes requests. `debounceTime` waits for a pause, `distinctUntilChanged` skips the same value, and `switchMap` avoids two saves overlapping.

## Example

```text
this.form.valueChanges.pipe(
  debounceTime(800),
  distinctUntilChanged((a, b) => JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b)),
  switchMap(v => this.api.saveDraft(v)),
  takeUntilDestroyed(this.destroyRef)
).subscribe(() => this.savedAt.set(new Date()));
```

## When to use it

Use it for long forms where losing work would hurt.

topics.title: Scenario: The app crashes with "window is not defined" after enabling SSR. What would you do?
Scenario: You must upgrade an Angular app by two major versions. What is your plan?
topics.body:
## Know it

Upgrade one major version at a time with `ng update`, read the update guide, fix breaking changes, update third-party libraries, and run the build and tests after every step.

---

## Explanation

Skipping versions causes hard-to-trace failures. `ng update @angular/core @angular/cli` runs migrations for you. Check that libraries (Material, NgRx) support the new version and that Node and TypeScript versions match.

## Example

```text
git checkout -b upgrade-18
ng update @angular/core@17 @angular/cli@17
npm test && ng build
ng update @angular/core@18 @angular/cli@18
npm test && ng build
```

## When to use it

Use it for questions about maintaining a long-lived project.

topics.title: Scenario: A component is hard to unit test because it calls a service that calls the API. How would you test it?
Scenario: A page needs data from three APIs, but one depends on the result of another. How would you combine them?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use `switchMap` (or `concatMap`) for the dependent call, and `forkJoin` for the independent calls, then combine them in one stream.

---

## Explanation

If B needs A's result, B must wait for A. C does not depend on anything, so it can run in parallel. Mixing both keeps the page as fast as possible.

## Example

```text
vm$ = this.api.getUser().pipe(
  switchMap(user => forkJoin({
    user: of(user),
    orders: this.api.getOrders(user.id),     // depends on user
    settings: this.api.getSettings()          // independent, runs in parallel
  }))
);
```

## When to use it

Use it for pages assembled from several backend calls.

topics.title: Scenario: A button triggers an API call and users click it many times. How would you prevent duplicate requests?
Scenario: Child components all need the same configuration object. What are your options?
topics.body:
## Know it

Provide it once with an `InjectionToken` or a service, and let children `inject` it, instead of passing it down through every `@Input`.

---

## Explanation

Passing a value through many levels ("prop drilling") makes components depend on each other's structure. DI lets a component ask for what it needs, and you can override the provider for a subtree.

## Example

```text
export const THEME = new InjectionToken<Theme>('THEME');

@Component({ providers: [{ provide: THEME, useValue: darkTheme }] })   // a subtree override
export class DashboardComponent {}

private theme = inject(THEME);   // any child component
```

## When to use it

Use it for configuration, themes, and feature flags that many components share.

topics.title: Scenario: Two services need each other and Angular reports a circular dependency. How do you solve it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Remove the cycle by moving the shared logic into a third service, or by using events/Observables instead of direct calls. Use `Injector` for lazy lookup only as a last resort.

---

## Explanation

A circular dependency usually shows the responsibilities are mixed. Extract the shared part so both services depend on it, not on each other.

## Example

```text
// before: AService <-> BService
// after:  AService -> SharedService <- BService

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class SharedService { /* the logic both needed */ }
```

## When to use it

Use it as the default answer; it also improves testing.

topics.title: Scenario: A search handler fires on every keystroke. How would you write your own debounce function?
Scenario: A loop creates buttons with setTimeout and every one prints the same number. Why?
topics.body:
## Know it

With `var`, all callbacks share one variable, so they all see its final value. Using `let` gives each loop iteration its own variable.

---

## Explanation

`var` is function-scoped, so the loop has a single `i`. The callbacks run later, after the loop ended and `i` is 3. `let` is block-scoped, so each iteration gets a new binding.

## Example

```js
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log('var', i), 0);
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log('let', j), 0);
// var 3, var 3, var 3
// let 0, let 1, let 2
```

## When to use it

Use `let` and `const` by default; this is a classic closure question.

topics.title: Scenario: You have a list with thousands of buttons and need click handling without thousands of listeners. What would you do?
Scenario: You must call an API for 20 ids, but only 5 requests may run at a time. How would you do it?
Scenario: An expensive function is called repeatedly with the same arguments. How would you speed it up?
Scenario: An API returns deeply nested arrays and you need one flat list. How would you flatten it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use `Array.prototype.flat(depth)`; use `Infinity` for any depth. For arrays of objects with child arrays, use `flatMap`.

---

## Explanation

`flat` removes one level by default. `flatMap` maps and flattens one level in a single step, which is handy for "orders contain items".

## Example

```js
console.log([1, [2, [3, [4]]]].flat(Infinity));          // [1, 2, 3, 4]

const orders = [{ id: 1, items: ['a', 'b'] }, { id: 2, items: ['c'] }];
console.log(orders.flatMap(o => o.items));               // ['a', 'b', 'c']
```

## When to use it

Use it when combining results from several lists or API pages.

topics.title: Scenario: A heavy loop freezes the page. How would you keep the UI responsive?
Scenario: A fetch request may hang for a long time. How would you add a timeout and cancel it?
Scenario: You need an exact copy of a nested object. Why is the spread operator not enough?
topics.body:
## Know it

Spread makes a shallow copy: nested objects are still shared with the original. For a deep copy use `structuredClone`.

---

## Explanation

`{ ...obj }` copies the top level only, so changing `copy.address.city` also changes the original. `structuredClone` copies nested data (dates, maps, sets), but not functions. `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` loses dates, `undefined`, and functions.

## Example

```js
const original = { name: 'Ram', address: { city: 'Pune' } };

const shallow = { ...original };
shallow.address.city = 'Delhi';
console.log(original.address.city);     // Delhi  (shared!)

const deep = structuredClone({ name: 'Ram', address: { city: 'Pune' } });
deep.address.city = 'Agra';
console.log(deep.address.city);         // Agra, the source is not affected
```

## When to use it

Use deep copies before editing nested data that is displayed elsewhere.

topics.title: Scenario: A sort puts "10" before "2" and names with accents in the wrong place. How do you sort correctly?
topics.body:
## Know it

`sort()` converts items to strings by default, so numbers need a compare function. For text with accents or different cases, use `localeCompare`.

---

## Explanation

Default sorting compares UTF-16 text, so "10" comes before "2". A compare function returning `a - b` sorts numbers. `localeCompare` follows language rules.

## Example

```js
console.log([10, 2, 33, 4].sort());                 // [10, 2, 33, 4]  (wrong, as text)
console.log([10, 2, 33, 4].sort((a, b) => a - b));  // [2, 4, 10, 33]

console.log(['é', 'e', 'z', 'a'].sort((a, b) => a.localeCompare(b)));   // [a, e, é, z]
```

## When to use it

Use it any time a table or dropdown must be sorted for users.

topics.title: Scenario: One failed request inside Promise.all rejects everything. How would you still get the successful results?
Scenario: A function must run only once, even if it is called many times. How would you write it?
Scenario: A screen has loading, success, and error states. How would you model them safely in TypeScript?
Scenario: A value arrives as unknown from JSON.parse. How do you use it safely?
Scenario: You wrote the same fetch wrapper for many endpoints with different return types. How would you type it?
topics.body:
## Know it

Make the wrapper generic: `get<T>(url): Promise<T>`. The caller says what type to expect, and the result is typed without repeating the function.

---

## Explanation

A generic is a type parameter, like a variable for a type. Remember that the type is a promise by the caller; for untrusted data, still validate at runtime.

## Example

```ts
async function get<T>(data: T): Promise<T> {          // stands in for an HTTP call
  return data;
}

interface User { id: number; name: string }
get<User>({ id: 1, name: 'Ram' }).then(u => console.log(u.name));   // Ram
get<number[]>([1, 2, 3]).then(n => console.log(n.length));          // 3
```

## When to use it

Use it for API services, caches, and reusable helpers.

topics.title: Scenario: You need an object type where every property is read-only, including nested ones. How would you create it?
topics.body:
## Know it

`Readonly<T>` makes only the top level read-only. For nested objects, write a recursive mapped type such as `DeepReadonly<T>`.

---

## Explanation

A mapped type loops over the keys of a type. Making it recursive applies `readonly` to every level. The check happens at compile time only; at runtime use `Object.freeze` if you need protection.

## Example

```ts
type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] };

interface Config { api: { url: string }; retries: number }
const cfg: DeepReadonly<Config> = { api: { url: 'https://x.com' }, retries: 3 };
// cfg.api.url = 'y';   // compile error: cannot assign to 'url' (read-only)
console.log(cfg.api.url, cfg.retries);   // https://x.com 3
```

## When to use it

Use it for configuration and state that must not be changed by accident.

topics.title: Scenario: You want a config object checked against a type but still keep its exact literal values. What would you use?
Scenario: Should you use an enum or a union of string literals for a set of values?
topics.body:
## Know it

For most Angular code, a union of string literals (or a `const` object) is simpler and has no runtime cost. Use an enum when you need a runtime object to loop over or reverse-map.

---

## Explanation

Regular enums generate JavaScript code and numeric enums allow surprising values. Unions are erased at compile time and work well with JSON from APIs.

## Example

```ts
type Role = 'admin' | 'user' | 'guest';
const can = (r: Role) => r === 'admin';
console.log(can('admin'));          // true

const Role2 = { Admin: 'admin', User: 'user' } as const;      // runtime values + a type
type Role2 = typeof Role2[keyof typeof Role2];
console.log(Object.values(Role2));  // [ 'admin', 'user' ]
```

## When to use it

Use unions for most cases; use a `const` object or enum when you need to list the values.

topics.title: Scenario: A function behaves differently depending on its argument type. How can TypeScript express that?
Scenario: Two ids are both numbers, but passing a user id where an order id is expected must be an error. How would you do it?
Scenario: You need the return type of an existing function without writing it again. What would you use?
topics.body:
## Know it

Use the `ReturnType<typeof fn>` utility type. For promises, combine it with `Awaited`.

---

## Explanation

It keeps your types in sync with the function, so changing the function updates the type automatically. `Parameters<typeof fn>` does the same for the arguments.

## Example

```ts
function createUser() { return { id: 1, name: 'Ram', active: true }; }

type User = ReturnType<typeof createUser>;
const u: User = { id: 2, name: 'Sita', active: false };
console.log(u.name);                         // Sita

async function load() { return [1, 2, 3]; }
type Loaded = Awaited<ReturnType<typeof load>>;   // number[]
const list: Loaded = [4, 5];
console.log(list.length);                    // 2
```

## When to use it

Use it for derived types such as service results and store state.

topics.title: Scenario: A map of settings must have a value for every key of a union. How can TypeScript enforce it?
What is the difference between any and unknown in TypeScript?
topics.body:
## Know it

`any` switches type checking off; you can do anything with it. `unknown` is the safe version: you must narrow it before you can use it.

---

## Explanation

Because `any` spreads silently, bugs appear at runtime. `unknown` forces a check, so errors appear at compile time. Prefer `unknown` for untrusted input.

## Example

```ts
const a: any = 'text';
try { a.toFixed(2); } catch (e) { console.log('any crashed at runtime: not a number'); }   // the compiler did not warn

const u: unknown = 'text';
if (typeof u === 'string') console.log(u.toUpperCase());   // TEXT   (allowed after narrowing)
// u.toUpperCase();                                          // compile error without narrowing
```

## When to use it

Use `unknown` for parsed JSON, caught errors, and external data; avoid `any`.

items.question: What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript?
items.answer: var is function-scoped, while let and const are block-scoped. let can be reassigned, but const cannot be reassigned. I generally use const by default and let when a variable needs to change.

items.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
items.answer: == compares values after type conversion when needed, while === compares both value and type without type conversion. I generally use === to avoid unexpected conversions.

items.question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
items.answer: undefined usually means a value has not been assigned, while null is an intentional empty value. They are different values, so null === undefined is false.

items.question: What is the difference between map(), filter(), and forEach()?
items.answer: map() transforms each element and returns a new array. filter() returns a new array containing elements that pass a condition. forEach() runs a callback for each element and does not return a transformed array.

items.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
items.answer: A closure is created when a function remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after the outer function has finished. Closures are useful for keeping state and creating private variables.

items.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous code?
items.answer: Synchronous code runs one statement at a time and waits for each statement to finish. Asynchronous code allows work such as API requests or timers to complete later without blocking the rest of the program.

items.question: What is the difference between a Promise and an Observable?
items.answer: A Promise typically provides one eventual success or failure result. An Observable can emit multiple values over time and can be managed with RxJS operators; it starts when subscribed to in common RxJS usage.

items.question: What is the event loop in JavaScript?
items.answer: The event loop coordinates synchronous code with queued asynchronous callbacks. Synchronous code runs first, then queued microtasks such as Promise callbacks run before the next timer task such as setTimeout.

items.question: What is the difference between call(), apply(), and bind()?
items.answer: call() invokes a function immediately with arguments passed individually. apply() invokes it immediately with arguments in an array. bind() returns a new function with this set, which can be called later.

items.question: What is the difference between map(), filter(), and reduce()?
items.answer: map() transforms every element and returns a new array. filter() returns all elements that match a condition. reduce() combines the elements into one accumulated result, such as a total.

items.question: What is the difference between find() and filter()?
items.answer: find() returns the first matching element, or undefined if there is no match. filter() returns a new array containing every matching element, or an empty array if there are no matches.

items.question: What is the difference between spread and rest?
items.answer: Spread expands an array or object into individual elements or properties. Rest collects remaining values into an array or object, such as collecting function arguments. Both use the ... syntax, but their purposes differ.

items.question: What is destructuring in JavaScript, and when would you use it?
items.answer: Destructuring lets us extract values from arrays or properties from objects into variables. It makes code shorter and easier to read, for example const { name, role } = user.

items.question: What is the difference between ngOnInit() and ngOnChanges()?
items.answer: ngOnInit() runs once after Angular initializes the component's input properties. ngOnChanges() runs when an input-bound property changes, including during the initial input setup. Use ngOnChanges() when logic must react to changing @Input() values.

items.question: What happens if you mutate an object passed to an OnPush component?
items.answer: Changing a property on the same object does not change its reference, so an OnPush child may not detect the input change. Create a new object or array reference to make the update detectable.

items.question: What is the difference between ViewChild and ViewChildren, and when can you access them?
items.answer: ViewChild queries one matching element or child component, while ViewChildren queries multiple matches. ngAfterViewInit() runs after the component's view has initialized, so it is a suitable lifecycle hook for accessing view queries.

items.question: What is an InjectionToken in Angular?
items.answer: An InjectionToken lets Angular's dependency injection system provide a value that does not have a class type, such as configuration or an interface-based dependency. It gives that dependency a unique token to inject.
